Background Ampulla of Vater (AoV) carcinoma is a malignancy arising from the ampulla of Vater, the anatomical convergence of the common bile duct, pancreatic duct, and duodenum. This unique anatomical location gives rise to both histological and molecular heterogeneity, reflecting contributions from intestinal and pancreatobiliary lineages. AoV carcinoma is often categorized into intestinal and pancreatobiliary subtypes, which exhibit distinct prognostic and therapeutic characteristics [ 1 , 2 ]. However, this binary classification does not fully account for the molecular diversity and variable clinical behavior observed among patients [ 3 ]. Previous genomic studies have provided important insights into the molecular landscape of AoV carcinoma. Notably, Yachida et al. [ 4 ] identified frequent mutations in the ELF3 gene, implicating it as a potential driver of tumorigenesis. Similarly, Gingras et al. [ 5 ] reported recurrent ELF3 inactivation and widespread dysregulation of the WNT signaling pathway. While these studies advanced our understanding of AoV carcinogenesis, they were based on whole-exome sequencing and bulk transcriptome profiling, which lack the resolution to capture cell type-specific transcriptional programs and the complexity of tumor-microenvironment interactions. As a result, the biological basis of epithelial heterogeneity and the functional contributions of non-malignant cell populations remain poorly understood. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers a powerful approach to address these limitations by enabling high-resolution, cell-type-resolved transcriptomic profiling [ 6 ]. This technology facilitates the identification of cellular subpopulations, and intercellular communication networks that are not accessible through bulk sequencing methods. Despite its potential, scRNA-seq has not yet been applied to AoV carcinoma, leaving fundamental gaps in our understanding of its cellular and transcriptional architecture. Therefore, our study is essential to move beyond bulk-level genomic insights and establish a high-resolution, cell-type-resolved atlas of AoV carcinoma. In this study, we present the first single-cell transcriptomic analysis of AoV carcinoma. Using scRNA-seq on primary tumor specimens, we identify distinct epithelial subtypes characterized by unique oncogenic and reveal their associations with the immune landscape and clinical outcomes. This work establishes a foundational single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma and provides new insights into its cellular diversity with potential translational implications. Methods Study patients This study included 70 patients histologically diagnosed with AoV adenocarcinoma between September 2005 and March 2023 at Samsung Medical Center (SMC), of whom eight underwent single-cell RNA sequencing and 62 underwent bulk RNA sequencing. Patient demographics and clinical characteristics, including age, gender, tumor stage according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition, tumor differentiation, adjuvant chemotherapy administration, and survival data, were retrospectively collected. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board at SMC (IRB No. SMC-2022–06-076) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided written informed consent for the future research use of their pathology specimens. Single-cell RNA sequencing Fresh tumor and adjacent normal tissue specimens were obtained from patients with AoV carcinoma before treatment through Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for scRNA sequencing. Acquired tissues are collected in MACS® Tissue Storage Solution (Miltenyi Biotec., Auburn, CA, USA) on ice and processed to the single cell dissociation immediately. Biopsy tissues are placed on a petri dish with a small volume of enzyme mixture solution (Tumor Dissociation Kit, Miltenyi Biotec.) and minced into small pieces under 1–2 mm with surgical blades. Minced pieces are transferred to gentleMACS TM C-tube containing enzyme mixture solution. By choosing an appropriate program of gentleMACS TM Dissociator, tissue pieces are further dissociated three times with two interval incubations for 30 minutes at 37 °C under continuous rotation using the MACSmix TM Tube Rotator. Resuspended samples are applied to a cell strainer (70 μm) and washed with 10 ml of DMEM/F12 media with 1% FBS. After a centrifugation at 400xg for 5 minutes, cells were resuspended in an appropriate volume of media and counted with trypan blue staining or acridine orange/propidium iodide staining. Optionally, erythrocytes are removed by red blood cell lysis solution for 10 min before counting. We initiated the cell preparation process by employing the LUNA-FL™ Automated Fluorescence Cell Counter (logos biosystems). Detailed guidelines for cell preparation were sourced from the 10x Genomics Single Cell Protocols Cell Preparation Guide and the Guidelines for Optimal Sample Preparation flowchart. Libraries were meticulously constructed using the Chromium controller in accordance with the 10x Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3’ v3.1 protocol (10x Genomics). In brief, cell suspensions were diluted in nuclease-free water, aiming to achieve a targeted cell count of 10,000. The diluted cell suspension was mixed with a master mix and subsequently loaded onto a Chromium Next GEM chip, along with Single Cell 3’ V3.1 gel beads and partitioning oil. Within the droplets formed in the chip, RNA transcripts from individual cells underwent unique barcoding and reverse transcription. Pooled cDNA molecules then underwent sequential processes, including end repair, addition of a single ‘A’ base, and adapter ligation. Subsequently, the resulting products were subjected to purification and enrichment through polymerase chain reaction (PCR), ultimately yielding the final cDNA library. To ensure library quality and quantify the purified libraries, we adhered to the qPCR Quantification Protocol Guide (KAPA). Furthermore, library qualification was performed using the Agilent Technologies 4200 TapeStation from Agilent Technologies. The sequenced libraries were processed using the HiSeqX platform from Illumina to obtain the requisite data for our study. Data preprocessing and quality control Raw sequencing data were processed using CellRanger (v7.0.1; 10x Genomics) [ 7 ], with alignment to the GRCh38 reference genome via STAR. CellBender (v 0.2.2) [ 8 ] was applied to each sample to eliminate background RNA contamination. Doublets were detected using Scrublet (v 0.2.3) [ 9 ], with thresholds determined according to simulation-derived scores. we excluded low-quality cells with fewer than 500 detected genes and a mitochondrial gene proportion exceeding 20%. Seurat (v4.3.0) [ 10 ] was used for downstream processing, including normalization, variable gene selection, scaling (regressing out total UMI counts, mitochondrial gene proportion, and cell cycle scores), principal component analysis, and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) projection. Clustering was performed using the FindNeighbors and FindClusters functions, with dimensionality assessed via JackStraw and ElbowPlot methods. Cell type annotation was conducted using SingleR (v2.0.0) [ 11 ] and further validated through the expression of canonical lineage markers. Major cell types were identified using EPCAM (epithelial cells), COL1A1 (fibroblasts), VWF (endothelial cells), CD3D (T cells), CD14 (myeloid cells), and CD79A (B cells). For more granular annotation of immune and stromal subsets, we utilized the following marker sets: CD4 for helper T cells, CD8 for cytotoxic T cells, FOXP3 for regulatory T cells (Tregs), and NCAM1 and NCR1 for NK cells. Myeloid sub-populations were defined by C1QC (macrophages), LYZ and S100A9 (monocytes), CD1C (dendritic cells), and CPA3 and KIT (mast cells). B cell lineages were further distinguished using CD79A and MS4A1 (B cells), CD38 and CD27 (plasma cells). Subclustering analyses were performed on major immune and stromal compartments following additional doublet removal [ 12 ]. Identification of epithelial subtypes using cNMF To identify transcriptional programs within epithelial cells, we applied consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) (v0.2) [ 13 ] to the normalized gene expression matrix. The number of components (k) was varied from 2 to 15, and the optimal solution was selected based on silhouette scores and Frobenius reconstruction error. Copy number variation inference To infer copy number alterations at the single-cell level, CopyKAT (v1.1.0) [ 14 ] was applied with default parameters. T cells were used as a reference for normal diploid profiles. CNV scores were computed for individual epithelial cells and summarized across samples to evaluate subtype-specific genomic instability. Transcription factor regulatory network inference Regulatory network analysis was performed using the pySCENIC (v0.12.1) [ 15 ] pipeline. Regulon activity scores were computed from raw UMI matrices to identify transcription factor-target gene modules, and average activity scores were calculated per subtype for downstream comparative analyses. Modular score and stemness estimation The CytoTRACE algorithm (v0.3.3) [ 16 ] was used to infer the differentiation potential of malignant epithelial cells. CytoTRACE computes transcriptional diversity and expression correlation to derive stemness scores, ranging from 0 (fully differentiated) to 1 (highly undifferentiated). This approach enables the identification of less differentiated, stem-like cell states at single-cell resolution. To evaluate functional characteristics of epithelial subtypes, including stemness potential, we calculated gene module scores using AddModuleScore function in the Seurat package. This approach determines the average expression of a specific gene program at the single-cell level, which is then normalized by subtracting the aggregated expression of control feature sets. To ensure a robust baseline, all analyzed features are binned based on their average expression levels, and control features are randomly selected from each bin. This process effectively accounts for technical noise and the influence of overall gene expression profiles. The stemness gene set was constructed using previously reported stemness-associated markers [ 17 ]. Functional enrichment analysis Differentially expressed genes were selected based on adjusted p -values and fold changes. Functional enrichment analysis was performed using EnrichR (v3.2) [ 18 ], employing the hypergeometric test with default parameters to identify overrepresented pathways and biological processes. We employed the hypergeometric test with default parameters to identify overrepresented pathways and biological processes from the MSigDB Hallmark gene set collection. Cell-cell communication analysis Ligand-receptor interaction analysis was conducted using CellPhoneDB (v5.0.0) [ 19 ] to identify potential intercellular communication events between cell types. Significant interactions were inferred via permutation testing using default parameters. Pseudotime trajectory analysis To infer the developmental hierarchy of epithelial subtypes, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis using the Monocle2 R package (v2.30.0) [ 20 ]. To minimize potential biological variations across patients, we utilized the integrated data generated via the FindIntegrationAnchors and IntegrateData functions from the Seurat package. For trajectory ordering, we selected the top 30 differentially expressed genes from each epithelial cluster. Dimensionality reduction was performed using the DDRTree algorithm. Bulk RNA sequencing and processing For bulk RNA sequencing, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor tissues from an independent cohort of surgically resected 62 AoV carcinoma patients were analyzed. Transcript-level quantification was achieved using RSEM (v1.3.0) [ 21 ], aligned to the GRCh38 genome with GENCODE v33 annotation. Gene-level expression matrices were derived for integrative analyses with single-cell data. Proportions of each subtype were estimated in bulk RNA-seq samples using MuSiC (v1.0.0) [ 22 ]. Xenium in situ hybridization and spatial analysis Surgically resected FFPE tissue samples from AoV tumor patients were profiled using Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Panel (10x Genomics). FFPE tissue sections (5 µm) were prepared on Xenium slides using Xenium Prime Sample Preparation Reagents. RNA quality was assessed by calculating the percentage of RNA fragments > 200 nucleotides (DV200) extracted from tissue sections, and H&E staining were also used to assess tissue morphology and region of interests by a specialized pathologist before performing the Xenium in situ hybridization. Slides were deparaffinized, rehydrated and decrosslinked, followed by hybridization with Xenium 5K Priming Oligos and probes targeting messenger RNA. Probes were ligated, amplified and washed, with subsequent antibody staining for cell segmentation. Autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining were performed and slides they were stored in phosphate-buffered saline with tween-20 (PBS-T) at 4 °C. The Xenium Analyzer (version 3.1) was used for imaging, decoding, segmentation and cell assignment, following the manufacturer’s protocols. During the initial quality control and filtering step, cells with a transcript count below 100 were classified as low-quality and excluded from all downstream analyses. For cell type classification, we utilized our own scRNA-seq dataset as the reference. Cell assignment was performed using the FindTransferAnchors and TransferData functions within the Seurat package, employing default parameters. Cells with a prediction score below 0.5 were classified as unknown and excluded from further downstream analyses. Survival analysis The clinical relevance of epithelial subtypes was evaluated using survival analysis. Kaplan-Meier curves were generated using the survival and survminer R packages (v0.5.2). Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression models were implemented using the coxph function to assess associations with overall survival and disease-free survival. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed in R. Pair-wise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were utilized to analyze the proportional differences between groups within each cell type/subset. Significance is displayed as *, p  < 0.05; **, p  < 0.01; and ***, p  < 0.001. For comparisons among multiple groups, the Kruskal-Wallis test was used to determine global significance, followed by Dunn’s test for pairwise post-hoc comparisons with adjustments for multiple testing. Statistical significance for multiple comparisons is presented as adjusted p -values (Padj), indicated as follows: *, Padj < 0.05;, Padj < 0.01; and ***, Padj < 0.001. Pearson correlation was employed to calculate the correlation between the proportions of each pair of cell subsets, and Spearman correlation was used for the co-ecosystem analysis. Results Patient characteristics This study included 70 patients (scRNA-seq: n  = 8 and bulk RNA-seq: n  = 62) with AoV carcinoma. Median age was 61.5 years (range, 36–83 years) and 33 were male (47.1%). Tumor stage (AJCC 8th edition) was I-III in the majority of patients (67/70, 95.7%), with only one patient classified as stage 0 and two as stage IV. During a median follow-up of 9.7 years (interquartile range, 6.4–12.7 years), 27 deaths (38.6%) occurred (Table S1 ). Single-cell transcriptomic profiling reveals diverse cellular composition in AoV carcinoma To investigate the cellular architecture of AoV carcinoma, we performed scRNA-seq on tumors ( n  = 8) and matched adjacent normal tissues ( n  = 4) (Fig. 1 a). After quality filtering, a total of 34,672 cells were analyzed and grouped into 18 clusters, which were subsequently classified into six major cell types based on cell type marker gene expression (Fig. 1 b–c). UMAP visualization revealed that while immune cells were broadly shared across patients, epithelial cell clusters displayed strong patient-specific transcriptional profiles, consistent with the absence of batch effects and reflecting inter-patient variation driven by tumor-specific copy number alterations [ 23 , 24 ] (Fig. 1 d). We further examined the distribution of cell types across individual samples, revealing substantial inter-patient heterogeneity in cellular composition (Fig. 1 e). Some tumors were highly enriched in epithelial or myeloid populations, whereas others showed greater T cell infiltration. These findings highlight the cellular complexity of AoV carcinoma and underscore the diversity of tumor-immune microenvironments across patients. Bar plots display relative proportions of each major cell type Epithelial subtyping reveals distinct transcriptional programs and inter-patient heterogeneity To investigate epithelial heterogeneity in AoV carcinoma, we performed subclustering of epithelial cells. This analysis revealed strong patient-specific clustering patterns (Fig. 2 a), indicating pronounced transcriptional differences between tumors. We then applied consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) to the epithelial transcriptomes, identifying four robust molecular subtypes (NMF-1 to NMF-4) (Fig. S1 a-b). Although each subtype included epithelial cells from multiple patients, their relative proportions varied markedly across samples (Fig. 2 b). This suggests that, while certain transcriptional programs are shared among tumors, their dominance is highly patient-specific, reflecting substantial inter-patient heterogeneity. Fig. 2 Identification and characterization of transcriptional subtypes in AoV carcinoma. ( a ) UMAP visualization of epithelial cells from AoV tissues ( n  = 8), color-coded by patient sample. ( b ) Proportional composition of four transcriptional subtypes (NMF-1 to NMF-4) in each AoV tumor, identified by consensus non-negative matrix factorization (cNMF) clustering of epithelial transcriptomes. ( c ) Violin plots showing expression levels of well-known marker genes associated with AoV subtypes: CDX2 and KRT20 (intestinal subtype), MUC1 and KRT7 (pancreatobiliary subtype). ( d ) Functional enrichment analysis of each transcriptional subtype, visualized as a bubble plot. The pathways were identified using the MSigDB hallmark gene set collection. The size of each dot represents the statistical significance (-log 10 adjusted p -value), and the color denotes the corresponding transcriptional subtype We further examined the expression of established AoV subtype marker genes across the four subtypes (Fig. 2 c). Intestinal markers ( CDX2 and KRT20 ) were strongly expressed in NMF-1 and NMF-3, whereas pancreatobiliary markers ( KRT7 and MUC1 ) were predominantly enriched in NMF-2. These findings support the biological relevance of the identified subtypes and their alignment with previously described histological features [ 2 , 25 ]. Functional enrichment analysis revealed distinct transcriptional programs characterizing each subtype (Fig. 2 d and Table S2 ): NMF-1 was enriched for Wnt/β-catenin signaling (designated Int-Wnt), NMF-2 for KRAS signaling (PB-KRAS), NMF-3 for hypoxia-related pathways (Int-Hypoxia), and NMF-4 for cell cycle-associated signatures (Cycling). We categorize these four programs as three lineage-driven, differentiated subtypes and one progenitor/functional subtype (NMF-4, Cycling). To further characterize the regulatory landscape underlying epithelial heterogeneity, we performed regulon activity analysis across epithelial cells. This analysis revealed that multiple transcription factor regulons were differentially activated in a subtype-specific manner (Fig. S1 c). MSX1 activity was predominantly elevated in the Int-Wnt subtype compared to the PB-KRAS and Cycling subtypes. HNF1B activity reached its highest levels in the PB-KRAS subtype, showing a significant increase over the Cycling subtype and a strong upward trend compared to the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes. SIRT6 activity was notably enriched in the Int-Hypoxia subtype, while CDX1 was most active in the Cycling subtype, significantly surpassing the levels in the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia groups (Fig. S1 d). The MSX1 is a known WNT/β-catenin responsive transcription factor implicated in promoting intestinal tumorigenesis [ 26 ]. Similarly, the enrichment of HNF1B in the PB-KRAS subtype is relevant, as its overexpression has been shown to enhance the expression of liver progenitor cell markers and stemness in liver cancer cells [ 27 ]. Finally, the activation of the SIRT6 regulon in the Int-Hypoxia subtype is consistent with its known role in enhancing the stability of HIF-1α, a process linked to epithelial-mesenchymal transition under hypoxic conditions [ 28 ]. These regulon profiles were concordant with the transcriptional programs defined by cNMF, further supporting the molecular distinction among AoV epithelial subtypes. Collectively, these results demonstrate that epithelial cells in AoV carcinoma exhibit diverse transcriptional states driven by lineage-specific and oncogenic programs, with subtype composition varying substantially between tumors. PB-KRAS subtype exhibit distinct genomic instability and stem-like properties To interrogate the degree of genomic instability underlying each epithelial subtype, we first analyzed copy number variation (CNV) profiles inferred from single-cell transcriptomes. Notably, CNV patterns were strongly patient-specific, indicating inter-patient variability in genomic alterations (Fig. 3 a). At the single-cell level, CNV scores were markedly elevated in tumor epithelial cells compared to non-epithelial controls, with the PB-KRAS subtype exhibiting the highest levels of genomic aberrations (Fig. S2 a). To validate these findings at the sample level, we averaged CNV scores across epithelial cells within each sample and compared them across subtypes. This analysis confirmed that the PB-KRAS subtype exhibits the highest CNV burden among all epithelial subtypes (Kruskal-Wallis, p  = 0.00013; Fig. 3 b). These results indicate that genomic instability is unevenly distributed among AoV epithelial subtypes and is particularly pronounced in PB-KRAS subtype. For pairwise post-hoc comparisons, Dunn’s test was used to adjust for multiple comparisons. *Padj < 0.05, ** Padj < 0.01, *** Padj < 0.001; n.s., not significant Given that high genomic instability is frequently associated with aggressive phenotypes and enhanced self-renewal capacity [ 29 ], we next investigated the functional and developmental hierarchy of these subtypes. Based on its highest CNV burden, we specifically focused on evaluating the stem-like properties of the PB-KRAS subtype. We first focused on the Cycling subtype. Given its cell cycle-associated transcriptional program and the enrichment of progenitor-associated regulons, such as CDX1 (Fig. S1 d), we hypothesized that it represents a less differentiated, progenitor-like state. To infer the developmental potential across all subtypes, we employed CytoTRACE [ 16 ], a computational tool that infers developmental potential using transcriptional entropy. As expected, the Cycling subtype exhibited high CytoTRACE scores (Fig. 3 c and Fig. S2 b), supporting its identity as a less differentiated, progenitor-like state. Surprisingly, the PB-KRAS subtype, which otherwise presents as a differentiated lineage, exhibited the highest CytoTRACE scores (Fig. 3 c and Fig. S2 b), suggesting unexpected stem-like features. This combination—a seemingly differentiated state with high developmental potential—defines a non-canonical stemness phenotype. This suggests that, unlike the canonical progenitor-like Cycling subtype, the PB-KRAS subtype represents a distinct, highly aggressive stem-like epithelial state that deviates from the typical differentiation pathway. To further examine this possibility, we calculated stemness scores based on a curated stem cell gene signature [ 17 ]. The PB-KRAS subtype exhibited elevated stemness scores that were comparable to those of Cycling cells, while remaining notably higher than the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes (Kruskal-Wallis, p  = 0.00043; Fig. 3 d and Fig. S2 c). To provide dynamic evidence of this developmental hierarchy, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis using Monocle2 [ 20 ]. The resulting trajectory delineated a clear lineage progression originating from the Cycling subtype, passing through the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtype, and ultimately culminating in the PB-KRAS subtype at the terminal end (Fig. 3 e). Notably, despite its terminal position on the pseudotime axis—which typically denotes a fully differentiated state—the PB-KRAS subtype harbored exceptionally high developmental potential, consistent with its elevated CytoTRACE (Fig. 3 f) and stemness scores (Fig. 3 g). This paradoxical terminal stemness suggests that PB-KRAS cells do not merely follow a conventional differentiation path but may undergo a coordinated transcriptional reprogramming or de-differentiation process, re-acquiring progenitor-like properties at an advanced stage of lineage development. We next sought to determine the potential molecular drivers of this phenotype, focusing on KRAS , the defining feature of the PB-KRAS subtype. Expression of KRAS was significantly upregulated in PB-KRAS subtype compared to the Int-Wnt subtypes (Fig. 3 h and Fig. S2 d), whereas CNV at the KRAS locus showed no significant difference among the subtypes (Fig. 3 i). Consistent with this, correlation analysis at the sample level revealed a moderate positive correlation between CNV score and stemness score ( r  = 0.5, p  = 0.014, Fig. S2 e). Furthermore, the expression of KRAS showed a strong positive correlation with both stemness score ( r  = 0.6, p  = 0.002, Fig. S2 f) and CNV score ( r  = 0.59, p  = 0.002, Fig. S2 g). These findings collectively highlight the robust association of both genomic instability and KRAS expression with the enhanced stem-like properties of the PB-KRAS subtype. Since KRAS knockdown in pancreatic cancer cells is known to reduce stemness characteristics [ 30 ], these observations suggest that the transcriptional upregulation of KRAS , rather than genomic alterations, is the likely contributor to the stemness signature of the PB-KRAS subtype. Epithelial subtypes confer distinct prognostic significance and clinical relevance in AoV carcinoma To evaluate the clinical significance of the four epithelial subtypes (Int-Wnt, PB-KRAS, Int-Hypoxia, and Cycling), we first deconvoluted their proportions in bulk RNA-seq profiles from 62 AoV carcinoma samples using the single-cell-derived subtype signatures. Among these, the Int-Wnt subtype was the most abundant, followed by Int-Hypoxia and PB-KRAS, whereas the Cycling subtype was relatively rare across samples (Fig. 4 a and Table S3 ). ( e-f ) Forest plots from Cox proportional hazards models showing hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals for each clinical and molecular variable in analyses of OS ( e ) and disease-free survival ( f ) We then assessed whether subtype proportions were associated with clinical variables. PB-KRAS subtype proportions were significantly elevated in patients who experienced recurrence ( p  = 0.011; Fig. S3 a), whereas no significant differences were observed across genders, adjuvant chemotherapy or tumor stages (Fig. S3 b-d). Regarding tumor stage, the Int-Hypoxia subtype was found to be more prevalent in Stage I tumors compared to Stage II (Padj = 0.045; Fig. S3 d). Next, we examined the prognostic impact of each subtype on OS. Proportions of Int-Wnt subtype was positively correlated with OS ( r  = 0.4, p  = 0.001) (Fig. 4 b), while PB-KRAS subtype abundance was negatively correlated with survival ( r  = −0.34, p  = 0.007) (Fig. 4 c). Int-Hypoxia subtype showed a weaker and non-significant inverse correlation ( r  = −0.21, p  = 0.097) (Fig. 4 d). Kaplan-Meier analyses further demonstrated that high PB-KRAS subtype content was significantly associated with worse survival ( p  = 0.001), while high Int-Wnt subtype content showed a trend toward improved survival ( p  = 0.013). To determine whether AoV subtypes independently contribute to prognosis, we performed multivariate Cox regression analyses incorporating clinical covariates. Notably, PB-KRAS subtype was significantly associated with worse OS (hazard ratio; HR = 116.6, 95% confidence interval; CI = 5.4–2496.6, p  = 0.002) and DFS (HR = 101.1, 95% CI = 3.3–3132.4, p  = 0.008), independent of other factors (Fig. 4 e–f), while Int-Wnt subtype was significantly associated with improved prognosis (DFS: HR = 0.1, 95% CI = 0.004–0.7, p  = 0.028) (Fig. 4 f). Consistently, univariate Cox regression analyses supported the prognostic significance of PB-KRAS subtype for both OS and DFS (Fig. S3 e-f). Together, these findings highlight that the composition of epithelial subtypes, particularly PB-KRAS and Int-Wnt subtype, has significant prognostic and clinical relevance in AoV carcinoma. The PB-KRAS subtype is associated with a most distinctly aggressive phenotype and a higher likelihood of recurrence. This analysis revealed 13 distinct clusters, which were annotated based on canonical marker genes and differentially expressed gene analysis (Fig. 5 a, b). These clusters included various helper T (Th), regulatory T (Treg), cytotoxic T (Tc), and natural killer (NK) cell subsets (Fig. S4 a). At the single-cell level, the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells was strongly correlated with the abundance of PB-KRAS subtype within each tumor ( r  = 0.98, p  < 0.001; Fig. 5 c). These Tc- GZMK cells represent a pre-dysfunctional state of CD8 + T cells [ 31 ], characterized by the robust expression of effector molecules such as GZMK and the absence of terminal exhaustion markers like HAVCR2 , while exhibiting moderate levels of early activation markers such as LAG3 (Fig. S4 a). This association was further validated in bulk RNA-seq data, where higher PB-KRAS subtype proportions were positively correlated with Tc- GZMK proportions across patients ( r  = 0.26, p  = 0.037; Fig. 5 d). These results suggest a potential interaction between PB-KRAS subtype and Tc- GZMK cells. We also examined whether their abundance was associated with clinical outcomes. Patients with high Tc- GZMK cell proportions exhibited significantly worse OS compared to those with lower levels (Fig. 5 e). We next explored potential epithelial-immune crosstalk using ligand-receptor interaction analysis. PB-KRAS subtype exhibited enriched interactions with Tc- GZMK cells through multiple ligand-receptor axes, including TGFB2 , SPP1 , and FGF2 , which are well-known mediators of immunosuppressive signaling (Fig. S4 b). These factors are associated with T cell exhaustion, suppression of cytotoxic responses, and immune evasion, suggesting that PB-KRAS subtype may contribute to shaping a dysfunctional yet Tc- GZMK -rich immune microenvironment. Spatial profiling reveals an immunosuppressive microenvironment in PB-KRAS subtype regions To investigate the spatial relationships between cellular subtypes and the tumor microenvironment, we performed Xenium in situ analysis on two representative AoV carcinoma samples, categorized as intestinal type and pancreatobiliary type based on the consensus judgment of experienced pathologists examining the tumor sections (Fig. 5 f). We first used single-cell RNA sequencing to estimate the major cell types and then mapped their spatial distribution across the tissue (Fig. 5 g). To investigate subtype-specific spatial patterns, we next identified and distinguished specific regions within the tumors, focusing on the AoV-ST1 sample, which are characterized by high proportions of Int-Hypoxia, and the AoV-ST2 sample, which are characterized by high proportions of the PB-KRAS subtype (Fig. 5 h). Importantly, the classification of regions derived from scRNA-seq mapping into Int-Hypoxia high (AoV-ST1) and PB-KRAS high (AoV-ST2) categories showed strong agreement with the initial pathological classification. Visualization of the spatial maps revealed a striking co-localization between the PB-KRAS subtype and Tc-GZMK cells (indicated by triangle-shaped dots), with a denser infiltration observed in the PB-KRAS high sample (Fig. 5 h). Quantitative analysis confirmed this observation: the PB-KRAS high sample exhibited a markedly higher proportion of PB-KRAS cells (among all epithelial cells) and a corresponding elevation in the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells (among all T cells) compared to the Int-Hypoxia high sample (Fig. 5 i). To further validate the spatial association between these populations, we performed a nearest neighbor distance analysis using the Xenium spatial coordinates. Our results revealed that Tc- GZMK cells were located significantly closer to PB-KRAS cells, with a mean minimum distance of 114.3 µm, whereas the distance to Int-hypoxia cells was nearly three-fold higher at 321.4 µm (Fig. 5 j). To visually confirm the presence of the Tc- GZMK population, we performed multiplex immunofluorescence using MACSima Imaging System ( n  = 3 per each group; see supplementary methods). Although this population was relatively sparse, pancreatobiliary subtype enriched samples showed higher infiltration of Tc- GZMK cells, whereas intestinal subtype dominant tumors displayed sparse Tc- GZMK infiltration (Fig. S5 a-b). Quantification confirmed that the proportion of Tc- GZMK cells was significantly higher in Pancreatobiliary subtype compared to intestinal subtype tumors ( p  = 0.0375; Fig. S5 c). These initial findings collectively suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype is associated with a distinctive and highly infiltrated tumor microenvironment. PB-KRAS subtype associates with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment To gain deeper insights into the immune microenvironment of AoV carcinoma, we conducted detailed subclustering analyses specifically focusing on myeloid and B lineage cells. This allowed us to resolve cellular heterogeneity within these immune compartments. Myeloid cells were classified into distinct subpopulations including macrophages, monocytes, dendritic cells (DCs), and mast cells based on canonical lineage markers and differentially expressed genes (Fig. 6 a), with neutrophils excluded from this analysis because they were predominantly derived from a single sample (Fig. S6 a-b). Similarly, B lineage cells were divided into naive B cells and multiple subsets of plasma cells, each characterized by unique transcriptomic signatures (Fig. 6 b). These refined annotations enabled a more precise characterization of cell-type-specific contributions to the tumor microenvironment. Fig. 6 Tumor microenvironmental associations of PB-KRAS subtype in ampulla of Vater (AoV) carcinoma. ( a-b ) UMAP plots showing clustering and annotation of myeloid and mast cell subsets ( a ) and B/plasma cell ( b ) subsets based on marker gene expression. ( c ) Heatmap showing pairwise spearman correlations between the proportions of tumor subtypes and immune cell subsets inferred from scRNA-seq data. * p  < 0.05, ** p  < 0.01, *** p  < 0.001 To assess the relationship between epithelial subtypes and immune cell populations, we performed correlation analysis across epithelial and immune cell proportions. Notably, the PB-KRAS subtype exhibited strong positive correlations with macrophage- SPP1 and Tc- GZMK clusters (Fig. 6 c). SPP1 -expressing macrophages have previously been associated with immunosuppressive and pro-tumorigenic functions [ 32 , 33 ]. In addition to the T cell infiltration, the spatial distribution of pro-tumorigenic myeloid cells also exhibited a marked preference for the PB-KRAS-rich environment. The nearest neighbor distance analysis demonstrated that macrophage- SPP1 were predominantly localized in close proximity to the PB-KRAS subtype, with a mean distance of 352.6 µm, compared to a significantly larger distance of 903.0 µm from the Int-hypoxia subtype (Fig. 5 j). To investigate the molecular mechanisms that may underlie this observation, we conducted a formal cell-cell communication analysis between epithelial subtypes and myeloid subclusters. This analysis identified several significant signaling axes, including PTN-ALK, FGF2–FGFR1, and FGF19–FGFR1, which were specifically enriched in the interaction between the PB-KRAS subtype and SPP1 + macrophages (Fig. S6 c). Notably, FGF2 is a well-established mediator known to promote the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages toward a pro-tumorigenic, M2-like state within the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment [ 34 ]. These findings provide molecular evidence that the PB-KRAS subtype actively modulates the functional phenotype of the myeloid compartment, offering a mechanistic basis that extends beyond mere numerical correlation. These findings suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype may develop within, or contribute to, a uniquely immunologically conditioned microenvironment enriched in tumor-promoting macrophages and pre-dysfunctional CD8 + T cells. This immune landscape may underlie the aggressive behavior and recurrence-prone nature of this epithelial subtype. Further mechanistic studies are warranted to clarify the functional significance of these immune–epithelial interactions and evaluate their potential as therapeutic targets. Discussion This study presents the first single-cell transcriptomic analysis of AoV carcinoma, offering a high-resolution landscape of its epithelial and immune cell composition. Previous genomic investigations, primarily based on whole-exome sequencing, have significantly advanced our understanding of AoV carcinoma by identifying recurrent alterations such as ELF3 mutations and WNT pathway dysregulation [ 4 , 5 ]. However, these bulk approaches lack the granularity required to resolve cell type-specific programs and microenvironmental interactions. Our single-cell approach addresses these limitations and provides novel insights into epithelial heterogeneity, differentiation states, and tumor-immune crosstalk in AoV carcinoma. Among the four molecular subtypes identified, our data demonstrate that the intestinal subtype itself is not homogeneous but comprises at least two molecularly distinct programs: one characterized by active WNT/β-catenin signaling (Int-Wnt) and another driven by hypoxia-associated pathways (Int-Hypoxia). The Int-Wnt subtype was defined by robust expression of WNT target genes and selective activation of the MSX1 regulon. MSX1 is known to function downstream of WNT/β-catenin signaling, playing a key role in promoting intestinal tumorigenesis. Its loss suppresses ectopic crypt formation in Apc-deficient models, suggesting that MSX1 is a critical mediator of WNT-driven epithelial transformation [ 26 ]. These features suggest that the Int-Wnt subtype retains a proliferative, WNT-responsive phenotype reminiscent of early intestinal neoplasia. In contrast, the Int-Hypoxia subtype displayed prominent enrichment of hypoxia-related gene sets and strong activation of the SIRT6 regulon. This suggests a mechanism involving SIRT6-enhanced stability of HIF-1α, which is known to promote the expression of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)-related transcription factors like SNAIL and TWIST [ 28 ]. The resultant overexpression of SNAIL and TWIST leads to suppression of E-cadherin and induction of Vimentin, hallmark events of EMT [ 28 ]. This molecular cascade facilitates increased cellular plasticity and motility, thereby promoting invasive behavior. EMT has been associated with enhanced metastatic potential and poor recurrence-free survival in several cancers, including papillary thyroid carcinoma, and may similarly portend aggressive clinical behavior in the Int-Hypoxia subtype of AoV carcinoma. By uncovering both a WNT-driven and a hypoxia-induced EMT program within the intestinal group, our analysis emphasizes the subtype’s underlying complexity and suggests that these distinctions may carry prognostic or therapeutic significance. The PB-KRAS subtype emerged as a particularly notable finding in our comprehensive epithelial subtyping. This subtype is defined by elevated KRAS expression and a transcriptional program robustly enriched for KRAS signaling. The PB-KRAS subtype exhibited a pronounced degree of genomic instability, carrying the highest CNV burden among all identified epithelial subtypes. Reflecting these substantial genomic aberrations, which are often associated with aggressive and self-renewal-enhancing phenotypes, we were guided to investigate its developmental hierarchy and specifically focused on evaluating its stem-like properties. Strikingly, the PB-KRAS subtype paradoxically exhibited high developmental potential and stemness scores, comparable to the canonical progenitor-like Cycling subtype. This unique combination of an apparent differentiated PB lineage state possessing high developmental potential defines a non-canonical stem-like epithelial state. Unlike the Cycling subtype, which represents a classical progenitor state, PB-KRAS cells achieve stemness through oncogenic signaling. Specifically, we found that the stemness signature was driven by the transcriptional upregulation of KRAS expression, independent of differential CNV at the KRAS locus. This suggests that elevated KRAS expression forces an aberrant, de-differentiated potential within a seemingly mature lineage. This is consistent with prior findings implicating KRAS signaling in the maintenance of stem-like features in pancreatic cancer cells [ 30 ]. Supporting this stem-like phenotype, HNF1B regulon activity was also selectively enriched in the PB-KRAS subtype. As HNF1B overexpression has been shown to enhance the expression of liver progenitor cell markers and stemness in liver cancer cells [ 27 ], this activation suggests a conserved role in supporting KRAS-associated epithelial states. Clinically, the PB-KRAS subtype was associated with significantly worse OS and DFS, as well as a higher incidence of recurrence. These findings collectively suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype program, defined by unique genomic instability and a KRAS-driven non-canonical stemness, represents the most clinically aggressive AoV subtype identified in this study, associated with poor outcomes and inherent therapeutic resistance. In addition to epithelial heterogeneity, our analysis revealed striking differences in the immune landscape across subtypes. PB-KRAS subtype were enriched for a distinct immune microenvironment characterized by abundant GZMK + CD8 + T cells (Tc-GZMK cells) and SPP1 + macrophages. GZMK enriched cytotoxic T cells, recently described as pre-dysfunctional T cells, represent an intermediate state preceding terminal T cell exhaustion [ 31 ]. Their accumulation within the PB-KRAS tumor microenvironment, coupled with spatial proximity to tumor epithelium and signaling through immunosuppressive ligand-receptor pairs (such as TGFB2 , FGF2 , and SPP1 ), strongly suggests active immune remodeling by tumor cells. These specific axes are known mediators of immunosuppressive signaling. For instance, TGF-β is known to suppress CD8 + T cell cytotoxicity by repressing a distinct program of cytotoxic gene responses, thereby limiting the antitumor immune response [ 35 ]. Similarly, FGF2 has been implicated in promoting T-cell exhaustion by regulating the expression of SPRY1 in esophageal tumor-infiltrating T cells, further impairing T cell function [ 36 ]. SPP1 directly suppresses CD8 + T cell proliferation and interferon-γ production, contributing to immune evasion by the tumor [ 37 ]. The co-enrichment of SPP1 + macrophages, previously implicated in promoting immune evasion and supporting tumor progression, further supports the presence of an immunosuppressive TME in PB-KRAS subtype. Importantly, high abundance of Tc-GZMK cells was associated with poor clinical outcomes, reinforcing the relevance of the immune milieu in disease progression. Taken together, our findings suggest that the PB-KRAS subtype defines a biologically aggressive, stem-like epithelial population that may either arise within or actively sculpt an immunosuppressive TME enriched for dysfunctional immune cell states. This epithelial-immune crosstalk may contribute to tumor recurrence and resistance to therapy. In contrast, the Int-Wnt and Int-Hypoxia subtypes are characterized by alternative oncogenic programs and immune environments, with divergent prognostic implications. A key limitation of this study is that the observed association between the PB-KRAS subtype and the immunosuppressive TME is based on correlational multi-omics analysis rather than direct functional validation. It is well established that activating KRAS mutations can actively modulate the immune microenvironment by promoting pro-tumorigenic macrophage polarization, inhibiting T-cell cytotoxicity, and accelerating T-cell exhaustion. Moreover, KRAS-mediated metabolic reprogramming may create a feedback loop where metabolite accumulation induces further genomic instability and mutational burden [ 38 ]. Although our findings regarding the PB-KRAS subtype are highly consistent with these known roles of KRAS signaling, further in vivo studies—such as orthotopic or syngeneic mouse models—and co-culture experiments are necessary to definitively prove the causal role of PB-KRAS cells in shaping this specific immunosuppressive niche. Moreover, while the specific ligand-receptor axes identified in this study, such as TGFB2 and SPP1, represent highly promising therapeutic targets, we acknowledge that their functional significance requires further validation in follow-up translational models utilizing functional blocking with neutralizing antibodies or small molecule inhibitors in patient-derived organoid-immune co-culture systems. These insights have potential therapeutic implications. Targeting the KRAS-HNF1B axis or the immunosuppressive mediators enriched in PB-KRAS subtype may offer novel avenues for treatment. Moreover, immunotherapeutic strategies aiming to restore CD8 + T cell functionality or reprogram tumor-associated macrophages may be particularly effective in this context. Future studies should focus on elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying epithelial-immune interactions in AoV carcinoma and evaluating their druggability in preclinical models. Additionally, although the multivariate analysis yielded an inflated hazard ratio due to complete separation in our small cohort ( n  = 62), Bootstrap validation (1,000 resamples) confirmed the statistical stability and robust prognostic value of the PB-KRAS subtype. Given the limited number of patients included in the single-cell analysis, validation in larger multi-institutional cohorts will be important to further establish the generalizability and potential clinical utility of the PB-KRAS subtype classification. Conclusions Our single-cell atlas of AoV carcinoma reveals profound epithelial and immune heterogeneity and identifies a clinically relevant PB-KRAS subtype defined by KRAS-driven non-canonical stem-like features and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. These findings provide a foundation for precision classification of AoV carcinoma and suggest novel therapeutic vulnerabilities for high-risk patients. title: Personalizing the treatment of head and neck cancer in vitro: The 3D-OTC model.
xenium_reason: Text indicates reuse of public Xenium data
evidence_text: Personalizing the treatment of head and neck cancer in vitro: The 3D-OTC model. BACKGROUND: Treatment of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) remains challenging and the survival rates of affected patients remain poor. A three-dimensional organotypic co-culture (3D-OTC) model where patient derived tumor tissue is cultured on human-derived fibroblasts (dermal equivalent, DE) was evaluated regarding its comparability to primary tumor tissue and its applicability in drug resistance testing. METHODS: 3D-OTC models were cultured from n = 10 HNSCC patients for up to 21 days. The growth pattern at the DE was compared to tumor budding of corresponding resection specimens. Furthermore, we immunohistochemically determined the immune cell infiltrate of primary tumor tissue and corresponding 3D-OTC models. Spatially resolved gene expression analysis (“Xenium in situ”) was performed for separate regions of interest within the 3D-OTC specimens and within primary tumor tissue. Up-regulated and down-regulated genes of the 3D-OTC samples were included in gene set enrichment analysis and up-regulated genes between invasive (invading the DE) and non-invasive tumor cells within the 3D-OTC samples were included in drug resistance testing using publicly available databases. RESULTS: The growth pattern observed at the DE was associated with tumor budding in primary tumor tissue. The density of CD3-/CD20-/CD56-positive cells was lower in 3D-OTC samples compared to primary tumor tissue. No such changes were observed for CD68-positive cells and no significant changes in the density of the immune cell infiltrate were detected during the cultivation period. The centroids and dispersion of the gene expression of the 3D-OTC samples did not differ from the corresponding primary tumor tissue. The regions of interest within the 3D-OTC samples showed distinct functional states in gene set enrichment analysis. The comparison of genes up-regulated in invasive tumor parts of the 3D-OTC samples could explain resistance of tumor subclones to certain chemotherapeutics. CONCLUSIONS: The 3D-OTC model morphologically and transcriptomically resembles primary tumor tissue and its biology while preserving the tumor microenvironment. Furthermore, the 3D-OTC model allows the standardized evaluation of tumor tissue by the definition of transcriptomically separate regions of interest and thus, could help to evaluate the impact of personalized therapeutic interventions on the tumor and its microenvironment in vitro.

evidence_text:
Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics reveal that the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis drives the immune-desert phenotype in small cell lung cancer by recruiting immunosuppressive CXCR4<sup>+</sup> neutrophils and S100A8<sup>+</sup> monocytes.

Background

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a recalcitrant malignancy with limited responses to immunotherapy, largely due to its uniquely immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). However, the molecular mechanisms driving this phenotype remain incompletely understood.

Methods

We integrated single-cell RNA sequencing and Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics to analyze the immune microenvironment of five SCLC and four non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) samples. Multiplex immunofluorescence was used to validate cell types and gene expression in the same tissue specimens, and animal models were employed to verify the key mechanistic pathway.

Results

SCLC displayed a distinct immune landscape compared with NSCLC, with increased infiltration of C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4)+ neutrophils (via neutrophil extracellular traps) and S100A8+ monocytes (toward an M2-like phenotype), and reduced CD8+ T-cell infiltration. Malignant epithelial cells in SCLC highly expressed CXCR4, regulated by transcription factors ISL LIM homeobox 1 and distal-less homeobox 5, which promoted immunosuppression. The C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12)-CXCR4 axis mediated competitive inhibition, impairing T-cell recruitment while enhancing neutrophil accumulation. Monocytes in SCLC shifted toward an M2-like phenotype, weakening antigen presentation. Xenium spatial transcriptomics confirmed colocalization of CXCR4+ neutrophils and S100A8+ monocytes with tumor cells at the tumor-normal interface, while CD8+ T cells were spatially segregated. In vivo experiments showed that CXCR4 inhibition reduced SCLC tumor growth, decreased immunosuppressive cell infiltration, and enhanced CD8+ T-cell accumulation.

Conclusions

The CXCL12-CXCR4 axis, together with immunosuppressive CXCR4+ neutrophils and S100A8+ monocytes, is a key driver of the immune-desert phenotype in SCLC. Targeting this axis holds promise as a therapeutic strategy to remodel the immunosuppressive TME and improve the efficacy of immunotherapy for SCLC. WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) has a highly immunosuppressive “immune-desert” tumor microenvironment (TME) and poor immunotherapy response. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) show limited efficacy, but the spatial/cellular mechanisms driving the immune-desert phenotype remain unclear, hindering targeted therapy development. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS We delineate a mechanism by which the C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12)–C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4 (CXCR4) axis drives the SCLC immune desert. First, ISL LIM homeobox 1/distal-less homeobox 5-driven tumor cells secrete CXCL12. Second, this recruits immunosuppressive CXCR4 + neutrophils and S100A8 + M2-like monocytes, leading to CD8 + T-cell exclusion and impaired major histocompatibility complex-I expression. Finally, CXCR4 inhibition therapeutically reverses these effects, curtailing tumor growth and enhancing antitumor immunity. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY This work provides a high-resolution SCLC TME map to guide CXCL12–CXCR4 research. Clinically, CXCR4 inhibitors may remodel TME and overcome ICI resistance. Practically, single-cell RNA sequencing/Xenium-based stratification can identify patients who benefit from CXCR4-targeted therapies, reducing ineffective treatment and advancing personalized care. Introduction Lung cancer (LC) has the highest global incidence and mortality. 1 Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) accounts for only approximately 15%–20% of all cases but is highly invasive with poor prognosis. 2 Although the introduction of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) has improved therapeutic outcomes to some extent, the overall response rate remains relatively low. 3 Therefore, comprehensive research on the pathogenesis of SCLC and its complex immune microenvironment is urgently needed. However, the molecular regulatory network of SCLC is highly complex, involving dynamic imbalances in gene expression, dysregulation of epigenetic modifications, cross-talk among multiple signaling pathways, and intricate interactions between immunosuppressive cells and tumor cells in the tumor microenvironment (TME), leading to limitations in subtyping accuracy and interpatient variability in treatment responses. 4 This complexity makes it challenging for analyses solely based on population-level molecular characteristics to comprehensively explain the mechanisms underlying SCLC initiation and progression and further complicates the accurate identification of potential therapeutic targets and drug resistance-related molecular events. Although ICIs have been incorporated into chemotherapy regimens in recent years, their clinical benefits remain limited. 5 From the perspective of the immune microenvironment, SCLC typically exhibits an immune-desert phenotype, characterized by extremely low infiltration of immune cells in the TME, low expression of immune checkpoint molecules, and frequent enrichment of fibrotic stroma and immunosuppressive cells, which together form a strong immunosuppressive barrier. 6 In contrast, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) frequently displays an immune-infiltrated phenotype, with infiltration of T and B cells and activation of immune checkpoint molecules in tumor tissues, suggesting active immune responses. 7 This distinction directly contributes to markedly different responses to immunotherapy between these two types of LC. The formation of the immune desert in SCLC may be related to the recruitment of immunosuppressive cells via chemokines secreted by tumor cells, whereas in the immune-infiltrated subtypes of NSCLC, immune escape more commonly relies on the activation of the programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1)/programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) pathway or T-cell exhaustion. Therefore, comparative studies on these two immune microenvironment subtypes may help reveal the specific mechanisms of immune escape in SCLC. The emergence of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) technology has provided a powerful approach to address these challenges. This method not only enables the resolution of transcriptomic profiles of immune, stromal, and tumor cells within the TME at single-cell resolution but also accurately identifies rare cell subpopulations that are undetectable by traditional bulk sequencing. 8 As an in situ spatial transcriptomic platform, Xenium enables subcellular, high-resolution spatial localization of hundreds of RNAs in intact tissues, allowing three-dimensional integrated analysis of “cellular phenotype–molecular characteristics–spatial location”. 9 The integration of scRNA-seq and Xenium not only precisely deciphers the gene expression profiles of individual cells but also defines their spatial context within the tissue. This combined approach holds promise for constructing a high-resolution single-cell atlas of the SCLC immune microenvironment, elucidating the cellular basis of immune desert formation, uncovering spatial interaction patterns between tumor cells and immune cell subsets, and identifying key signaling hubs that drive the development of an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Therefore, this study his study systematically dissected SCLC and NSCLC molecular characteristics via scRNA-seq/Xenium, characterized immune cell transcriptomes, validated spatial distribution via multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF), and verified key pathways in animal models to elucidate SCLC’s immune microenvironment and identify therapeutic targets. Results Global immune landscape in SCLC and NSCLC To comprehensively evaluate the immune landscape of SCLC, we collected nine tumor samples (five SCLC, four NSCLC) and performed scRNA-seq and in situ spatial transcriptomic analysis ( figure 1A ). After stringent filtering ( online supplemental Tables S1 and S2, Figure S1A-H ), 47,761 cells were obtained (24,133 NSCLC, 23,628 SCLC; figure 1B ), with 8 major cell types identified via marker genes: B cells (CD79A, JCHAIN), endothelial cells (CLDN5, CDH5), epithelial cells (EPCAM, KRT18), fibroblasts (DCN, PDGFRA), mast cells (CPA3, KIT), monocytes (LYZ, C1QA), neutrophils (CSF3R, FCGR3B), and T/NK cells (CD3D, NCAM1) ( figure 1C ). Cell cluster proportions were visualized ( figure 1D , S1I). χ 2 tests ( figure 1E ) and differential gene volcano plots ( online supplemental Figure S1J ) revealed significant differences in cell type composition between SCLC and NSCLC, with SCLC showing >twofold higher neutrophil proportion ( online supplemental Figure S1K ). Subset/marker expression was verified by scRNA-seq ( online supplemental Figure S1L ), and spatial distribution in tissue sections was examined via Xenium technology ( figure 1F , online supplemental Figure S2A and B ). Integrating Xenium and scRNA-seq data, we identified overlapping expressed genes, performed Pearson correlation analysis, and constructed heatmaps ( figure 1G , online supplemental Figure S2C ). Results showed significant consistency in cell type definition between the two methods, confirming Xenium’s reliability for studying LC cell composition and immune microenvironment. Figure 1 Global immune landscape in SCLC and NSCLC. ( A ) Schematic representation of the experimental design and analysis workflow. ( B ) UMAP plot showing sample groupings. ( C ) UMAP plot of eight cell types. ( D ) Violin plots of marker genes for the eight cell clusters. ( E ) Box plot of cell proportions. ( F ) Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomic staining of cell subpopulations. ( G ) Pearson correlation heatmap comparing scRNA-seq and Xenium in situ spatial transcriptome analyses. FF, fresh frozen; FFPB, formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded; LCA, lung cancer; NK, natural killer; NSCLC, non-small cell lung cancer; SCLC, small cell lung cancer; scRNA-seq, single-cell RNA sequencing; UMAP, Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection. Differences in epithelial cells between NSCLC and SCLC result in distinct immune microenvironments From LC samples, 16,779 epithelial cells were isolated and divided into three subsets ( figure 2A ). Using stromal/macrophage cells as references, inferCNV analysis classified cells with mean square >0.05 and correlation coefficient >0.5 as malignant, identifying 12,628 malignant cells ( figure 2B , online supplemental Figure S3A-C ). Proportion statistics ( online supplemental Figure S3D ) and χ 2 tests ( figure 2C ) revealed differential distribution of the three malignant subsets between SCLC and NSCLC: C1 (predominantly SCLC), C2 (SCLC-2 specific), and C3 (predominantly NSCLC). Signature gene analysis showed C1 enriched for C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4 ( CXCR4 ) and ISL LIM homeobox 1 ( ISL1 ), C2 for CDK6/HES5, and C3 for human leukocyte antigen ( HLA ) -A , HLA-B , and interferon-stimulated gene 15 ( ISG15 ) ( figure 2D ). In addition, SCLC also expressed ASCL1 , CD24 , CKB , CHGA , CXCR4 , TFF3 , ISL1 , and distal-less homeobox 5 ( DLX5 ) ( online supplemental Figure S3E ). Between SCLC and NSCLC, transcription factors ISL1/DLX5 were significantly activated in C1, with targets including CXCR4, suggesting SCLC may drive immune escape via ISL1-mediated CXCR4 overexpression. Differential gene analysis identified significantly upregulated CXCR4/ISL1 in SCLC ( figure 2E ). The results were visualized in a volcano plot ( figure 2F ), highlighting the top 20 upregulated and top 10 downregulated genes ( figure 2F ). Enrichment analysis showed SCLC upregulated genes linked to proliferation, drug resistance ( CKB ) 10 and endocrine function ( CHGA ), 11 while NSCLC upregulated genes related to TME immune regulation ( figure 2G ). Overlap between subset-specific signature genes and differentially expressed genes further validated subset functions. Quantitative set analysis for gene expression (QuSAGE) pathway analysis showed C1/C2 activated pathways associated with malignant progression (proliferation, mismatch repair, hypoxia), while C3 activated immune pathways (antigen presentation, natural killer (NK) cell cytotoxicity; figure 2H ), indicating NSCLC (C3) has stronger immune activity and SCLC (C1/C2) is immune-silent. SCENIC and differential gene analysis generated a ball-and-stick diagram. ISL1 was highly activated in C1, suggesting a key role in SCLC formation ( figure 2I ). Xenium spatial transcriptomics ( figure 2J , online supplemental Figure S4 ) and mIF staining ( figure 2K ) validated EPCAM + CXCR4 + cell distribution and expression. Xenium also verified some other key genes ( ASCL1, CHGA, CXCR4, ISL1 ; online supplemental Figure S4 ). In summary, important functional genes such as CXCR4 and ASCL1 are regulated by the same transcription factor, ISL1, which is a critical regulator of the neuroendocrine characteristics of SCLC, 12 whereas CXCR4 plays a pivotal role in tumor immune escape. 13 Figure 2 Proportion and distribution of CXCR4 + epithelial cells. ( A ) UMAP clustering of malignant cells. ( B ) UMAP plot of SCLC and NSCLC groups. ( C ) Box plot comparing cell proportions between SCLC and NSCLC groups. ( D ) Bubble plot of marker genes in C1, C2, and C3. ( E ) Violin plots showing CXCR4 and ISL1 expression in the two groups. ( F ) Volcano plot of differentially expressed genes between SCLC and NSCLC. ( G ) Bar plot of the top 15 differentially expressed proteins between SCLC and NSCLC. ( H ) Quantitative set analysis for gene expression pathway analysis in SCLC and NSCLC. ( I ) Ball-and-stick diagram showing transcription factors and their target genes. ( J ) Distribution and expression of CXCR4 + and ISL1 + epithelial cells detected using Xenium spatial transcriptomic analysis. ( K ) Immunofluorescence staining of CXCR4 + and ISL1 + epithelial cells. CXCR4, C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4; FC, fold change; FDR, false discovery rate; ISL1, ISL LIM homeobox 1; NSCLC, non-small cell lung cancer; SCLC, small cell lung cancer; UMAP, Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection. CXCR4 + neutrophils mediate immunosuppression in SCLC Using scRNA-seq, we identified a substantial number of infiltrating neutrophils in SCLC. These neutrophils expressed classic markers (G0S2, FCGR3B) and high CXCR4 levels ( figure 3A,B , online supplemental Figure S5 ), leading us to hypothesize their role in competitive immunosuppression—analogous to CXCR4 + tumor cells that inhibit T-cell infiltration. Further analysis of differential gene expression (DGE) between SCLC and NSCLC neutrophils revealed alterations in ten core genes. CD74: impaired immune recognition 14 ; IL1R2: downregulation reduces inflammatory responsiveness 15 ; LGALS3: alters immune cell function 16 ; interleukin (IL)-1 receptor-associated kinase 3: disrupts immune signal transduction 17 ; endoplasmic reticulum aminopeptidase 2: downregulation hinders T-cell recognition 18 ; IL-1 receptor antagonist: direct immunosuppression 19 ; protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type E: impairs immune activation 20 ; phosphodiesterase 4B: upregulation promotes tumor progression 21 ; prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 2: upregulation aids angiogenesis/immune evasion 22 ; matrix metalloproteinase 25: upregulation favors invasion/metastasis ( figure 3C ). 23 Collectively, these alterations indicate suppression of immune-activating functions, ultimately leading to immune silence. Figure 3 Immunosuppressive effects mediated by CXCR4 + neutrophils in SCLC. ( A ) UMAP plot showing sample distribution. ( B ) UMAP plot of marker genes. ( C ) Volcano plot of differentially expressed genes. ( D ) GO-Biological Process and pathway enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes. ( E ) Box plot of MHC-I scores and violin plots of associated molecules. ( F ) Pearson correlation analysis of neutrophil immune functions. ( G ) Expression and spatial distribution of CXCR4 , IFIT3 , and interferon-stimulated gene 15 in FCGR3B + neutrophils detected by Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics. ( H ) Multiplex immunohistochemistry staining showing CXCR2 and CXCR4 expression in CD66B + neutrophils. CXCR4, C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 4; FC, fold change; GO, Gene Ontology; KEGG, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes; HLA, human leukocyte antigen; MHC, major histocompatibility complex; NSCLC, non-small cell lung cancer; SCLC, small cell lung cancer; UMAP, Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection. Gene Ontology (GO)-Biological Process and pathway enrichment analysis showed upregulation of pro-inflammatory chemokines (IL-17, tumor necrosis factor (TNF)). Despite enhanced immune infiltration via strong chemokine binding, CXCR4 may bind C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12 (CXCL12) to competitively inhibit immunity, downregulating phagocytosis/antigen presentation. Downregulation of ferroptosis/autophagy pathways weakened tumor cell death mediation ( figure 3D ). Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecule expression in neutrophils was significantly reduced in SCLC: violin plots showed lower HLA-A/B/C/E/F ( figure 3E ), and box plot scoring revealed impaired antigen presentation/CD8 + T-cell activation—indicating immunosuppressive effects. In NSCLC, MHC class I, type II interferons (IFNs), and immune responses correlated positively with CXCR4. This correlation was absent in SCLC ( figure 3F ), confirming SCLC neutrophils’ immunosuppressive state. Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics identified FCGR3B + neutrophils, confirming increased CXCR4 + neutrophil infiltration in SCLC and decreased IFIT3+/ISG15+neutrophils ( figure 3G , online supplemental Figure S6 ). mIF staining further validated these findings ( figure 3H ). Distribution and significance of monocytes in SCLC and NSCLC groups To explore immune microenvironment differences between SCLC and NSCLC, monocytes as a key immune cell subset were investigated. Using scRNA-seq and bioinformatics analysis, we identified four monocyte subtypes from the two groups ( figure 4A ), with their distribution visualized via Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) dimensionality reduction ( figure 4B ).
