Discussion  In this paper, we presented DeSpaST, which is a graphic deconvolution model that integrates the cell morphology features from histology images with spatial transcriptomic data to predict the cellular resolution gene expression for cells across the tissue section. Unlike other methods that only enhance the ST resolution, DeSpaST stands out as the first model to directly infer cell-level gene expression from histology images and ST data. DeSpaST is innovative and beneficial in that it takes advantage of the histology images and explicitly models the spatial organization of cells. By constructing the cellular graphic structure, cell morphology and interaction information from histology images were successfully input to the GCN model as nodes and edges, respectively. GCN, with its capability to handle complex non-Euclidean structures, enables deconvolution at cell-level resolution by well aligning with the diverse and intricate cellular interaction topologies. We demonstrated the high accuracy, resolution, robustness, and efficacy of DeSpaST in this paper. This model can be easily applied to diverse types of tissues and ST data.  The cellular-level gene expression inferred from DeSpaST offers powerful support to many biomedical applications. In this study, we applied DeSpaST’s output to the spatial cell type annotation and inferred the pseudotime trajectories of tumor development. DeSpaST offers the cellular resolution for cell type identification compared to traditional spot-level cell type identification. DeSpaST clearly illustrates the cell types for individual cells, enabling the revelation of cell–cell interaction in the tumor microenvironment and providing valuable insights into tumor immunology studies. Pseudotime analysis further uncovers the pseudo-temporal trajectories of tumor progression, revealing distinct clusters of early- and late-stage cancer cells. The high precision of DeSpaST establishes a reliable foundation for subsequent spatial transcriptomics analyses, such as deriving differentially expressed genes and exploring cell–cell communication inference.  A key limitation of our evaluation is that the Xenium measurements used for validation are obtained from an adjacent FFPE section, rather than the exact same section profiled by Visium. Although adjacent-section validation is often necessary in practice because assays are destructive or mutually exclusive, it is inherently imperfect: consecutive sections can exhibit local tissue distortion during sectioning and mounting, cell displacement, partial-volume differences, and subtle microenvironmental heterogeneity (e.g. immune infiltration near boundaries). These factors can weaken strict quantitative comparability even when broad spatial trends remain visually similar. Therefore, the agreement we observe between DeSpaST predictions and Xenium should be interpreted primarily as qualitative and semi-quantitative evidence that DeSpaST recovers coherent spatial gene-expression patterns and microenvironmental structure, rather than as an absolute quantitative ground truth at single-cell resolution. To mitigate this limitation, we emphasize evaluations that do not require one-to-one cell correspondence across sections—such as region-level pattern concordance, marker-consistent localization, and spot-level correlations computed after aggregating predicted cells within each Visium spot—and we further assess whether predicted cell-level signals support consistent tissue organization using downstream spatial domain analyses.  Beyond the cross-section validation constraints discussed above, several additional limitations should be noted. First, DeSpaST’s accuracy depends on the upstream nucleus segmentation step; segmentation errors such as missed nuclei, over-segmentation, or misclassification propagate to the graph construction and deconvolution. Second, genes with very low or near-zero expression in the Visium data are inherently difficult to deconvolve, as there is minimal transcriptional signal to distribute among cells. Third, standardized simulation frameworks that jointly model realistic histology with spatially structured single-cell expression are not yet available, and matched single-cell spatial datasets with paired Visium and H&E inputs remain scarce, precluding direct ground-truth validation at single-cell resolution. Despite these limitations, DeSpaST demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple complementary evaluation criteria and tissue types.  In addition to uncovering cellular gene expression in ST data, DeSpaST holds the potential for deconvoluting cellular protein expression in spatial proteomics. Recently, numerous spatial proteomic methods have been developed to enable the direct detection of protein molecules with spatial variability. However, the resolution remains limited, typically operating at spot sizes around 20–100 μm [ 42–45 ]. The application of DeSpaST to improve the resolution of spatial proteomics encourages further exploration of spatially cellular protein expression.  DeSpaST is designed for broad applicability, leveraging histology images and ST data as input to uncover cellular-level expression. Its capabilities can be further extended by incorporating additional data sources. For example, if single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data are available from the same tissue or a similar sample, DeSpaST can integrate it as a cell type constraint, potentially improving the deconvolution accuracy. This is particularly valuable when dealing with very weak sequencing signals in ST data, as scRNA-seq offers higher sequencing depth. An additional enhancement for DeSpaST could involve its extension to 3D spatial transcriptomes. Recently, spatially resolved transcriptomic atlases in high-dimensional data have emerged to revolutionize the understanding of cell interaction and gene regulation within the organ. Organ-level 3D spatial transcriptomics [ 46–48 ] or proteomics [ 49 ] were reconstructed from serial 2D tissue sections. DeSpaST, with a potential 3D GCN version, could leverage these data’s complexity to learn 3D spatial cell features and deconvolute gene expression. This is particularly relevant as current 3D spatial transcriptomes often miss data between sections. DeSpaST can potentially address this gap and provide a more complete picture of the 3D spatial transcriptomic landscape.    Method   Datasets   Human breast cancer datasets 1  Two human breast cancer datasets were employed for constructing and validating the DeSpaST model. The first human breast cancer dataset consists of Visium ST data for DCIS and Invasive Carcinoma FFPE human breast cancer tissue. This dataset contains 2518 spots, with 5244 median genes per spot and a sequencing depth of 32 524 reads per spot.    Human breast cancer datasets 2  The second human breast cancer dataset is associated with a recently released Xenium  in situ  platform [ 25 ]. This research conducted a comprehensive analysis with three complementary technologies (Chromium, Visium, Xenium) on a single breast-cancer FFPE tissue. The Visium output ST data were used to deconvolute the cell-level gene expression using DeSpaST, which contains 4992 spots, with 5712 median genes per spot and 40 003 mean reads per spot. The Xenium panels were used as a reference standard to evaluate DeSpaST’s cell-level resolution prediction. Additionally, IF staining was performed after Xenium to assess the expression profiles of HER2 and CD20 proteins. The results from both the Xenium panel and the subsequent IF staining were then used to verify the effectiveness of DeSpaST.    Human ovarian cancer dataset  The human ovarian cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 4674 spots, with 8792 median genes per spot.    Human lung cancer dataset  The human lung cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 6195 spots, with 10 087 median genes per spot.     Spatial transcriptomics data preprocessing and image feature extraction  Spatial transcriptomics data were first preprocessed prior to analysis. Gene expression values in the spot barcode profile matrix were normalized to counts per million (CPM). To mitigate the impact of outliers, the normalized CPM values were scaled to the 95th percentile.  The cell morphology features were extracted from H&E images using HD-Staining (Histology-based Digital Staining of Pathology Images) [ 18 ], which is an automatic deep-learning model that simultaneously segments and classifies cell nuclei, as well as provides morphology information about each identified cell nucleus. The extracted morphological features encompassed the centroid position, cell area, convex area, eccentricity, extent, filled area, major axis length, minor axis length, orientation, perimeter, solidity, and probability. In addition, we further enriched DeSpaST by incorporating 1024-dimensional intermediate box features and 256-dimensional mask features derived from the HD-Staining model. These cell morphological features were incorporated into the construction of DeSpaST.    Cellular graphic structure construction  We initially divided whole-slide H&E images into 250 × 250-pixel patches centered on the Visium spots. In total, we generated 2518 patches for the 10× Visium human breast cancer dataset, 4992 patches for the Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] human breast cancer dataset, 4674 patches for the human ovarian cancer dataset, and 6195 patches for the human lung cancer dataset. For each patch, we first obtain each cell location by performing cell segmentation, then construct a directed graph structure by connecting the cells based on their spatial proximity. This graph structure was designed to incorporate at least eight nearest neighbors. Pairwise Euclidean distances between cell coordinates were computed to identify the nearest neighbors. For those patches with very low cell density (<8 cells), DeSpaST dynamically resized the patch to include at least eight neighboring cells. These directed graph structures captured the spatial relationship and connectivity among cells in the tissue.  Each graph structure consisted of two main components: nodes and edges. Nodes represent morphological features extracted through HD-Staining for individual cells. These node features have undergone global scaling as part of the preprocessing. Edges store information on edge categorization and edge spatial representation ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Edge categorization is determined based on the types of cells connected by each edge, which provides insight into the type of interactions between the connected cells. Here, we included a total of 49 combinations of edge categorizations across seven cell types ( Supplementary Fig. S2a ). Edge spatial representation refers to the spatial aspects of cell interactions, including the Cell Connectivity Angle and Spatial Proximity. Cell Connectivity Angle indicates the connectivity between neighboring cells and the directionality of these connections. Spatial Proximity reflects the physical distance between cells. Both nodes and edges collectively constitute the cellular graphic structure, which synergistically contributes to the definition of complex cellular relationships.    Auto graph convolutional network for spatial transcriptomics deconvolution  Following the construction of the cellular graphic structure and thoughtfully derived essential node and edge features, we employed dynamic edge-conditioned convolution to manage graphs of varying size and connectivity. This process is mathematically represented in Equation ( 1 ). The embedding vector of the convolution filter is then used to deconvolve the spot-level gene expression into cell-level gene expression. Our model-specific architecture comprises of three layers: two ECC (Edge-Conditioned Convolution) [ 50 ,  51 ] GCN layers [ 52 ,  53 ] followed by a ReLU activation function [ 54 ], and one linear transformation layer. Each ECC layer incorporates both node and edge feature embeddings for propagating information across the graph ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Image registration and result comparison   Immunofluorescence image and Xenium panel registration to hematoxylin and eosin images  In order to register the IF image and Xenium panel to the Visium corresponding H&E images and facilitate the comparison to the protein/RNA expression experiment, we employed skimage.transform package for image transformation. To achieve a precise and efficient registration, we systematically tested various combinations of angles and scales between the IF and H&E images. To optimize computing efficiency, we initially conducted tests with 10% scaled-down images to obtain approximate scale and angle adjustments. Subsequently, we fine-tuned the registration using the original scale.    DeSpaST model validation  We validate DeSpaST through the assessment of RNA expression and protein expression by utilizing data from the Xenium panel and IF images, respectively. Using the spatial information from Visium spot locations, we reconstructed the spot-level expression for DeSpaST, TESLA, Xenium panel, and IF protein expression. The accuracies of Visium ST data, TESLA, and the DeSpaST model were evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient with the Xenium panel and IF image.     Cell type analysis  To assign cell types to each predicted single cell, we adopted a fully automated cell-type identification algorithm, ScType [ 32 ], which utilizes the Xenium-tested marker gene as the selected cell markers. The cellular level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST was used as input. The Seurat package was used to normalize the data with the default LogNormalize method. We then use the Seurat FindNeighbors function with parameter dims = 1:50 and FindClusters function with resolution = 0.9, which results in 23 clusters. ScType was also applied with Xenium Breast Cancer Cell Marker panel. Each cluster was assigned to the cell type with the highest score, and clusters assigned the same cell type were merged into larger clusters.    Pseudotime analysis  The gene expression of tumor cells predicted by DeSpaST was extracted for pseudotime analysis. We first reduced the gene expression dimension using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, cell clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm, which is a fast approach to ensure that all cells are well connected for downstream optimal trajectory inference [ 55 ]. Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) [ 56 ] is used to construct a topological graph based on the cell partitions. The cluster with high expression of  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ], a gene marker of cancer stem cells, was selected as the trajectory root node. The Diffusion Pseudotime (DPT) method [ 57 ] was then applied to estimate pseudotime values, which represented the tumor cell dynamics. All analyses were performed using the SCANPY [ 58 ] Python packages.    Spatial domain detection  To assess whether each deconvolution method preserves biologically meaningful spatial structure at the domain level, we performed downstream spatial domain detection using the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as inputs. For each method, we first constructed two neighborhood graphs: (i) an expression kNN graph in a low-dimensional transcriptomic space, obtained by PCA on the predicted expression matrix and kNN graph construction using Scanpy, yielding an expression connectivity matrix       ; and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in the 2D coordinate space using Euclidean neighbors, yielding a symmetric binary adjacency matrix       . We then fused these graphs into a hybrid connectivity matrix via a linear combination,        where       balances spatial proximity and transcriptional similarity. Finally, we applied Leiden community detection on       to infer spatial domains for each tissue section, using identical processing across methods; all parameters are reported in the Supplementary Information. Domain assignments were benchmarked against manual domain annotations (when available) using Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI).    Key Points    DeSpaST introduces a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network for deconvolving spot-level ST data into true cell-level-resolution gene profiles.    DeSpaST integrates spatial and morphological features from histology images to model cell–cell organization and improve accuracy.    Extensively benchmarked across multiple cancer datasets, outperforming existing methods in resolution and precision.    DeSpaST enables diverse applications, including cell-type annotation, tumor trajectory analysis, and cell–cell communication discovery, demonstrating its potential to provide new insights in various biological contexts. Spatial Transcriptomics and Mechanisms of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-Associated Interstitial Nephritis Introduction  Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated acute interstitial nephritis (ICI-AIN) is the most common finding on histopathology among patients with ICI-associated acute kidney injury (ICI-AKI). Patients with ICI-AIN often have T cell-dominant infiltration of the kidney and high tissue levels of CXCR3 ligands such as CXCL9, 10, and 11; however, the mechanisms of inflammation in ICI-AIN are not well-understood.    Methods  We applied a subcellular spatial transcriptomics platform (Xenium Prime 5K) to compare the cellular composition of kidney biopsy tissue from patients with ICI-AIN with ICI-treated patients with acute tubular necrosis (ICI-ATN).    Results  Across 8 kidney biopsy specimens (4 with ICI-AIN, 4 with ICI-ATN), we analyzed 332,000 cells, comprising kidney parenchymal cells and infiltrating immune cells. Using a spatially aware cellular neighborhood-based classification, we identified cellular niches corresponding to each part of the nephron, in addition to unique fibrotic and inflammatory niches. Gene pathway analysis identified interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) and/or signal transducer and activator of transcription 1 (STAT1) signaling as strongly increased in ICI-AIN compared with ICI-ATN. Although all inflammatory niches were overrepresented in ICI-AIN, CD8+ T cell infiltration, and proinflammatory myeloid cells were the dominant immune niches. Spatial niche crosstalk analysis revealed that CD8+ T cell-derived IFN-γ likely induced a proinflammatory program in myeloid cells, with increased production of CXCL9, 10, and 11. Furthermore, IFN-γ signaling in ICI-AIN was associated with reduced oxidative phosphorylation in kidney tubular niches.    Conclusion  Spatial transcriptomics thus revealed novel insights into key differences in the pathophysiology of ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN, with IFN-γ-producing CD8 +  T cells as potential drivers of ICI-AIN.     Graphical abstract                        Keywords  acute interstitial nephritis  ICI-AKI  immune checkpoint inhibitor  interferon gamma  JAK-STAT1  spatial transcriptomics     pmc-status-qastatus  0    pmc-status-live  yes    pmc-status-embargo  no    pmc-status-released  yes    pmc-prop-open-access  yes    pmc-prop-olf  no    pmc-prop-manuscript  no    pmc-prop-legally-suppressed  no    pmc-prop-has-pdf  yes    pmc-prop-has-supplement  yes    pmc-prop-pdf-only  no    pmc-prop-suppress-copyright  no    pmc-prop-is-real-version  no    pmc-prop-is-scanned-article  no    pmc-prop-preprint  no    pmc-prop-in-epmc  yes    pmc-license-ref  CC BY-NC-ND       ICIs, which target programmed death (PD)-1, PD-ligand 1 (PD-L1), cytotoxic T-lymphocyte associated protein-4, and lymphocyte activation gene-3, release the brakes on the immune system and enhance its ability to destroy tumor cells. These drugs, which are now approved to treat > 20 cancer types, have dramatically improved outcomes for a number of malignancies. 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4  AKI is common in the setting of ICIs, with real-world studies showing that 15% to 25% of patients treated with ICIs develop AKI.  5   Although AIN is the most common histopathologic lesion seen in ICI-AKI,  6   ,   7   AKI can also occur because of non-ICI-related causes, including ATN. Distinguishing ICI-AIN from ICI-ATN is challenging without a kidney biopsy, because there are no clinical features specific to ICI-AIN.  6   Furthermore, the mechanisms underlying ICI-AIN are not well understood.  Recent studies have shown that proinflammatory cytokines like tumor necrosis factor, IFN-γ, and IFN-γ-induced chemokines such as CXCL 9, 10, and 11 are elevated in ICI-AIN but not in patients treated with ICI with AKI from other causes. 8 ,  9 ,  10  Single-cell transcriptomic analyses of tissue from patients with ICI-colitis  11   and myocarditis  12   have each identified an immune cell infiltration dominated by T cells and inflammatory myeloid cells, in addition to organ-specific differences, such as interleukin-17A-producing T cells in ICI-colitis.  In contrast to ICI-colitis and ICI-myocarditis, our understanding of the immune cell infiltrate, cellular interactions, and damage pathways in ICI-AIN is limited. Given the expanding indications for ICIs, the burden of disease of ICI-AIN is expected to increase.  13   ,   14   New insights into underlying mechanisms are urgently needed to improve the identification of at-risk patients, enable noninvasive diagnosis of ICI-AIN, and identify new therapeutic targets without inhibiting the antitumor response. Here, we utilized Xenium Prime 5K (10x Genomics, Pleasanton, CA), a novel spatial transcriptomics technology, to compare and contrast the cellular composition of kidney biopsy specimens from patients with ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN.   Methods   Patient Selection and Tissue Collection  We identified adult patients (≥ 18 years old) at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and/or Dana-Farber Cancer Institute who had received at least 1 dose of ICI therapy within 180 days before development of AKI (defined as a ≥ 1.5-fold rise in serum creatinine from pre-ICI baseline)  15   and who had a kidney biopsy performed for clinical purposes between 2021 and 2024. A total of 8 archival formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded kidney biopsies were obtained (4 with moderate-to-severe AIN and 4 with ATN, as adjudicated by 2 renal pathologists at Brigham and Women’s Hospital). All patients had consented to blood and urine collection, as well as archival tissue collection. Spatial transcriptomic analysis of archival tissue was conducted under institutional review board approved protocol (#2023P000393). Additionally, all patients had available urine proteomics data (Olink Target 96 Immuno-Oncology Panel and Olink Target 96 inflammation, with 140 unique proteins; Olink Proteomics, Uppsala, Sweden), as previously described.  8    This study was approved by the Brigham and Women’s Hospital and/or Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (21-685) and Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Boards (#2021P00044 and #2023P000393).    Xenium Slide Preparation  Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded blocks of kidney biopsies were sliced onto Xenium slides according to the “Xenium In Situ for Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded-Tissue Preparation Guide” ( CG000578  Rev C, 10x Genomics)  16   protocol. The Xenium slides were then prepared following the “Xenium In Situ for Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded-Deparaffinization and Decrosslinking” protocol ( CG000580  Rev D, 10x Genomics). In brief, the slides were incubated at 60 °C for 30 minutes and then sequentially immersed in xylene, ethanol, and nuclease-free water to deparaffinize and rehydrate the tissue. The Xenium slides were then immediately incubated in the decrosslinking and permeabilization solution at 80 °C for 30 minutes, followed by a wash with phosphate-buffered saline.  The Xenium slides were then processed according to the “Xenium Prime In Situ Gene Expression” user guide ( CG000760  Rev A, 10x Genomics) for the remaining slide preparation steps. The samples were hybridized with probes from Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue & Pathways Panel (PN-1000671, 10x Genomics) at 50 °C for 18 hours. After hybridization, the slides were washed and incubated with a ligation reaction mix, followed by another wash step and DNA amplification. Cell segmentation staining was then performed, and the slides were treated with an autofluorescence quencher and , 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole before loading into the Xenium instrument.    Xenium Analyzer Setup and Data Acquisition  Processed Xenium slides were loaded in the Xenium analyzer and imaged, following the guidelines in the “Xenium Analyzer User Guide ( CG000584  Rev F, 10x Genomics).” After scanning, the Xenium slides were removed from the Xenium analyzer and processed with post-run hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining according to the “Xenium In Situ Gene Expression-Post-Xenium Analyzer H&E Staining” protocol ( CG000613  Rev A, 10x Genomics).    Xenium Data Analysis  We performed both image-based segmentation using CellPose  17   and transcripts-based cell segmentation using Baysor (v0.7.1)  18   with the previous cell labels from the multimodal staining information. Then, we integrated the Xenium data with single cell RNA-seq reference atlas through Harmony and projected the labels using nearest neighbors, which are further curated with licensed nephrologists. Spatial domain clustering analyses were performed using the natural boundaries-based method, Tessera.  19   Niches were further identified using the  de novo  clustering analysis and manual curation, and further validated with the approximate positions of tissues on the H&E imaging. Downstream data analysis is described in more detail in the  Supplementary Methods .    Using Olink Data to Refine Transcriptomics Analyses  Using Olink data, we focused on proteins that we had previously shown to be differentially abundant in ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN.  8   ,   20   For proteins that were included in both the Inflammation and Immuno-Oncology panel, we used the results from the Inflammation panel. We performed pseudo-bulk aggregation of the transcripts per kidney biopsy by the AggregateExpression function in Seurat (v5.3.0)  21   and normalized expression levels to the biopsy area.     Results   Study Design and Cohort Description  We analyzed kidney biopsies of 4 patients with ICI-AIN and 4 with ICI-ATN using the Xenium Prime 5K (10x Genomics) spatial transcriptomics assay to measure  in situ  expression of 5001 genes ( Figure 1 a). Patients with ICI-ATN were chosen as the comparator, because they share potential confounders (malignant disease, cancer treatment, and unspecific kidney tissue changes caused by AKI); in the ICI-ATN cases, treatment with ICIs was not judged to be the cause of the AKI and often an alternative etiology was identified. Baseline demographics and characteristics of the AKI event are shown in  Supplementary Table S1 . Additional information on the kidney biopsy characteristics can be found in  Supplementary Table S2 . The time between AKI onset and kidney biopsy ranged from 2 to 18 days (median 7.5 days); all biopsies showed mild-moderate signs of irreversible damage and fibrosis (interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy range 10–40%).  Figure 1   Spatial transcriptomics identifies distinct cell states in ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN. (a) Study design and techniques involved. (b) Marker heatmap for the major cell types in spatial transcriptomic data. Rows show the cell types, columns show top selected markers, the size. (c) UMAP of spatial transcriptomic cells with cell type annotation in ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN, the size of the circle indicates the proportion of cells expressing the marker, the color indicates the average expression scale. (d) Differential abundance of cellular composition measured by ratio over all cells for both groups. (e) Cell type ratio in all patients of ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN, with corresponding color legend below. (f) Xenium cells from a representative patient with ICI-AIN. (g) Zoomed-in regions from F; multiple polygons show the segmented cells in their spatial position; colors of the polygons show the cell type; white dots with different shapes show the transcript positions. ICI-AIN, Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy-related acute interstitial nephritis; ICI-ATN, ICI therapy-related acute tubular necrosis; pDC, plasmacytoid dendritic cell; cDC1, conventional dendritic cell type 1; Collecting Duct-PC, (principal cells); Collecting Duct-IC, (intercalated cell); Immune (LowQ), Immune cell lineage cells with low quality data.                         Immune Cells in ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN  After cell segmentation and quality control ( Supplementary Figure S1 ), followed by label transfer and manual curation strategy, we identified a total of 332,341 cells (79% kept cells after quality control of resegmentation) with 21,251 to 66,751 cells per patient sample ( Supplementary Figure S1 ). Using curated cell types from the Kidney Precision Medicine Project atlas as a reference, we took 4875 overlapping high-quality genes between Xenium and Kidney Precision Medicine Project single-cell RNA-sequencing and jointly clustered the cells to define 24 major cell types. These cell types comprised both kidney parenchymal cells and immune cells across all 8 patient samples, expressing known biomarkers. The alignment performed well at the major lineage level ( Figure 1 b–c,  Supplementary Figure S1 ), as we observed high correlation of gene expression fold changes between the Kidney Precision Medicine Project atlas and our Xenium datasets ( Supplementary Figure S2–3 ), although the cell segmentation of cell types with complex, nonspheroidal geometries also led to spillover of transcripts into neighboring cells (e.g., in glomerular cell types).  Next, we applied covarying neighborhood analysis  22   to identify cell states strongly associated with ICI-AIN and found immune cells to be significantly expanded in ICI-AIN (global  P -value 0.02,  Figure 1 d). Compared with ICI-ATN, on average, ICI-AIN biopsies contained 27-fold more  XBP  high  plasma cells in ICI-AIN, 8-fold more  IL3RA  +  plasmacytoid dendritic cells, 7.9-fold more proliferating T cells, 7.6-fold more  FOXP3  + 
 CTLA4  +  regulatory T cells (Tregs), and 3.6-fold more  CXCL9  +  CIITA   +   inflammatory myeloid cells ( Figure 1 e,  Supplementary Figure S1 , false discovery rate < 0.05 for each). We also identified more kidney parenchymal cells in ICI-ATN, including SCNN1G+ collecting duct cells (2.2-fold higher),  PODXL  +  podocytes (3.4-fold higher),  KCNJ10  +  distal convoluted tubular cells (2.3-fold higher), and  CUBN  +  proximal tubular cells (2.1-fold higher), likely influenced by the variable sampling of kidney medulla during biopsies ( Supplementary Table S2 ). By mapping the cell types and individual detected marker transcripts in space, we were able to confirm the identified cell types in their spatial context, including high levels of  CD19  and  CD3E  transcripts in a large lymphoid aggregate,  PODXL  transcripts in glomeruli, and  CUBN  in proximal tubular cells ( Figure 1 f–g). In summary, we were able to characterize the immune cell infiltrate in ICI-AIN using spatial transcriptomics and identified a high density of plasma cells, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and T cells, among others.    Immune and Fibrosis Niches in ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN  To dissect cellular neighborhoods in their spatial context, we identified cellular niches using the Tessera package.  19   Tessera is an automated tissue-agnostic tissue segmentation method that introduces novel concepts of spatial cellular neighborhoods, or “niches,” delineates the tissues by closed multipolygons that aggregate spatially coherent cells, and approaches that infer the tissues’ edge with natural tissue boundaries. Tessera enables reducing the sparsity of spatial transcriptomic data and circumvents potential problems associated with cell segmentation methods by aggregating cells, thereby increasing the number of relevant transcripts per unit and decreasing misattribution errors. Using Tessera to characterize cellular niches in these biopsies, our approach enables us to identify potentially novel cellular niches and biologically meaningful architectural units within the spatial transcriptomic data. In total, we aggregated cells to 22,690 niches. Based on the clustering of these niches based on transcriptional similarities, we defined 9 major spatial niches, including immune, vascular, and fibrotic niches, and 6 kidney tissue-related niches ( Figure 2 a–d).  Figure 2   Immune and stromal cellular niches are expanded in ICI-AIN.  ( a) UMAP projection of niches using the aggregated gene expression in ICI-AIN patient group; each dot represents a tile with color showing different annotation of niche type. (b) UMAP for cells in ICI-ATN patient group, the legend as in A. (c) Heatmap of cell type ratio in each spatial niche, annotated color bar legend is the same as in A, the cell colors show the abundance of the cell type ratio. (d) Dot heatmap plot showing the marker average expression and expressed tile percentage. (e) multipolygon plot visualizes the spatial niches of one representative ICI-AIN patient, (f). same as E but for a patient with ICI-ATN. (g–h) marker expression in spatial niches for the same patient in E and F. (i) UMAP rendering which is colored by the covarying neighborhood analysis of spatial niches comparing ICI-AIN to ICI-ATN, red represents the increased niche abundance in ICI-AIN, blue depicts lower abundance. (j) UMAP showing the VCAM1+ niches across the 8 patients.                       The kidney-related niches included all major parts of the nephron—for example, glomerular niches were marked by high expression of  PODXL  and  WT1 . Similarly, we identified niches corresponding to the proximal tubule (with high expression of  CUBN  and  LRP2 ), loop of Henle (marked by  UMOD  and  CASR  expression), distal convoluted tubule (marked by  TRPM6  expression), and collecting duct (expressing  SCNN1G  and  HSD11B2  and combining both intercalated and principal cells;  Figure 2 d). Additionally, we identified niches associated with pathology; injured proximal tubular regions were marked by the expression of markers like  HAVCR1  (encoding kidney injury molecule 1) and  SOX9  in addition to the proximal tubule transcriptional signature, as has been extensively studied in the context of AKI. 23 ,  24 ,  25 ,  26  Immune niches contained different immune cell subsets; generally, we identified high levels of IFN-γ-induced transcripts like  SLAMF7 ,  CD38,  and  CXCL9 . Similarly, areas of fibrosis were marked by high expression of genes like  PDGFRA  and  COL5A1 .  The identity of the niches was confirmed by their cellular composition ( Figure 2 c), with the spatial expression of key marker genes following accurate niche distribution ( Figure 2 e–h).  We then applied covarying neighborhood analysis to characterize the cellular niches that were significantly expanded in ICI-AIN compared with ICI-ATN (global  P -value 0.03). We observed an expansion of immune fibrotic niches, as well as niches containing loop of Henle transcriptional profile in ICI-AIN, whereas the remaining kidney-specific niches were decreased in ICI-AIN ( Figure 2 i). The injured proximal tubule niche was more highly represented in ICI-ATN samples as marked by VCAM1+ niches ( Figure 2 j). Using a niche-based approach, we were thus able to identify all major parts of the nephron in addition to immune cell and fibrotic niches.    Immune Niche Subtyping Identifies Key Immunological Processes in ICI-AIN  To better understand the immune cell infiltration in ICI-AIN, we performed unbiased subclustering of the immune niches ( Figure 3 a). We confirmed key features of the ICI-ATN and ICI-AIN histopathology in serial sections ( Supplementary Figure S4 ). Some niches corresponded to the microenvironment of specific immune cells, such as plasma cell niches with high levels of transcripts as  FCRL5  and  TNFRSF17  (encoding B-cell maturation antigen) or plasmacytoid dendritic cells (expressing  LIL4RA , and  IL3RA  [encoding CD123]) ( Figure 3 b). The tertiary lymphoid structure (TLS)-like niches showed high expression of genes that are involved in the interaction of B and T cells, such as  CD28  and  ICOS , as well as their component cells. Other niches showed stronger transcriptional signals of the infiltrated kidney tissue or fibrotic processes in addition to an immune cell signature (termed “CD8 infiltrated kidney” and “inflammation with fibrosis”). We detected 2 separate types of myeloid cell niches, one with higher expression of proinflammatory genes (like  CSF2RB  and  MMP9 ) that are often associated with monocyte-derived cells, which we termed “myeloid inflammation,” and another myeloid niche type with increased expression of transcripts associated with tissue-resident or regulatory myeloid cells (such as  CD163 ,  MRC1  which encodes CD206, and  F13A1 ). Notably, T cell-related transcripts such as  CD3E  and  CD8A  were detected in all immune niches to varying degrees, highlighting the role of T-cell infiltration as a general feature of ICI-AIN. Compared with ICI-ATN, all immune niche subtypes were increased in ICI-AIN ( Figure 3 c). In a linear regression model examining the association of specific immune niches with ICI-AIN, all immune niche types were increased in ICI-AIN, with the strongest associations observed for the niche types “inflammatory myeloid”, “TLS-like” niches, and “CD8 infiltrated kidney” ( Figure 3 d). There was no association between “inflammatory myeloid” niche abundance and the time between AKI onset and kidney biopsy.    Distinct Chemokine Axes Underlie Immune Niche Subtype Heterogeneity  To better understand drivers of immune niche heterogeneity, we performed ligand-receptor analysis and observed greater overall ligand-receptor interaction strength across ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN ( Supplementary Figure S5 A and B). In both ICI-AIN and ICI-ATN, CXCL12-CXCR4, and CXCL9-CXCR3 interactions were observed in all patients, although the latter pair had higher strengths of association in ICI-AIN compared with ICI-ATN ( Supplementary Figure S5 C–F). CXCL12-CXCR4 was globally present in areas with myeloid inflammation, TLS, and plasma cells in ICI-AIN, whereas it was limited to a few niches in ICI-ATN.  Investigating the different immune subniches, expression of CXCR3 ligands CXCL9, 10, and 11 was observed in all subniches, but most prominently in the “myeloid inflammation” niches. This was associated with massive expansion of CXCR3-expressing cells ( Figure 3 e–f,  Supplementary Figure S5 G–J). The chemokine axes CCR7 and/or CCL19 and CXCR5 and/or CXCL13, both associated with B-T cell interaction and TLS, were most strongly detected in the TLS-like immune niches. CXCL12 was most strongly increased in plasma cell niches, as has previously been reported in bone marrow plasma cells.  27   Our analyses highlight the role of chemokines in the spatial organization of immune infiltrates in ICI-AIN, with CXCR3-CXCL9 interactions in areas of myeloid inflammation and CXCR5-CXCL13 interactions in TLS.    Spatial Transcriptomics Builds on Findings from Urine Proteomics  Building upon our previous urine proteomics analysis,  8   we compared paired aggregate gene expression and proteomic abundance of 5 differentially abundant proteins in ICI-AIN (CXCL9, CXCL10, CXCL11, FASLG, GZMA) and 1 in ICI-ATN (epidermal growth factor;  Supplementary Figure S6 ).  8   Mean aggregate transcript levels in ICI-AIN for these genes were changed in the same direction as the urinary protein abundance. Gene expression of  CXCL9, CXCL10, CXCL11,  and  GZMA  each completely separated the groups, often showing better separation than urine protein levels.    Gene Set Enrichment Analysis Identifies Interferon-Driven Responses in ICI-AIN  We next asked what signaling pathways contribute to the immune cell activation and tissue inflammation in ICI-AIN. Comparing differentially expressed genes within the niche types separately, IFN-γ-induced genes, such as  STAT1  and  CXCL9,  showed the strongest expression in ICI-AIN compared with ICI-ATN in most cellular niches ( Supplementary Figure S7 ). Gene set enrichment analysis of immune-related pathways in the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (RRID:SCR_012773) and Hallmark gene set collections similarly identified an increase in IFN-driven pathways (such as “Interferon gamma response”, “chemokine signaling”, “Janus Kinase-STAT”) in ICI-AIN ( Supplementary Figure S7 ). Especially within the tubular niches, including the injured proximal tubule, collecting duct and loop of Henle, we observed a strong reduction in the expression of genes related to oxidative phosphorylation in ICI-AIN. In summary, the IFN-γ response signature was the dominant transcriptional immune signature in ICI-AIN.    Tissue-Resident CD8 +  T Cells in ICI-AIN Produce IFN-γ and CXCL13  As we identified IFN-γ and/or STAT1 as the predominant signaling pathway and IFN-γ-induced genes as the top differentially expressed genes in ICI-AIN, we next investigated the cellular source of IFN-γ production. The greatest number of  IFNG  transcripts (75.1% of all  IFNG  transcripts identified in immune cells) were identified in CD8 +  T cells as compared with other immune cell subsets, including CD4 +  T cells ( Figure 4 a). Investigating differentially expressed genes within the CD8 +  T cells, we found  IFNG  to be one of the top upregulated genes in ICI-AIN ( Figure 4 b).  CXCL13  was also increased in CD8 +  T cells, as were markers of repeated activation, such as  PDCD1, LAG3,  and  CTLA4  in ICI-AIN CD8 +  T cells. Although ICI-ATN CD8 +  T cells expressed markers of short-lived effector T cells like  KLRG1  and  CX3CR1 , CD8 +  T cells in ICI-AIN showed higher levels of residency program markers like  ZNF683  (encoding HOBIT),  CXCR6,  and  ITGAE  (encoding CD103). Additionally, CD8+ T cells from patients with ICI-AIN were enriched for IFN-induced genes like  STAT1 ,  GBP1,  and  GBP5. As identified by gene set enrichment analysis, gene expression relating to oxidative phosphorylation was reduced in ICI-AIN samples, and tubular epithelial cells rely heavily on oxidative phosphorylation because of their high energy demand.  28   Using the spatial niche data, we found this reduction localized mostly to the niches related to parts of the kidney tubule ( Figure 4 c). The gene module score for oxidative phosphorylation was reduced in the injured as compared with the noninjured proximal tubule niches. However, in both injured and healthy proximal tubule niches in AIN samples, there was an additive reduction in oxidative phosphorylation gene signatures in multivariable linear regression models ( Supplementary Figure S8 ). IFN-γ-signaling within the noninjured proximal tubule niches was strongly anticorrelated with a gene signature for oxidative phosphorylation ( Figure 4 d).  Another hallmark effect of IFN-γ is the polarization of myeloid cells into a proinflammatory, tissue-aggressive state, as we observed in the “inflammatory myeloid” cluster ( Figure 3 a–b).  29   Within this cluster, we found the expression of genes typical for a proinflammatory myeloid polarization (such as  MMP9 ,  IDO1 ), as well as the highest gene expression signature of an IFN-γ response ( Figure 4 e–f). In summary, CD8 +  T cell-derived IFN-γ was associated with reduced oxidative phosphorylation in tubular cells and a proinflammatory signature in inflammatory myeloid cells.    Tissue-Resident Macrophage Niches Associate With Fibrosis  Finally, we investigated which immune cell niches were associated with fibrosis in ICI-AIN. To this end, we calculated the probability of neighboring an area of fibrosis for each subtype of immune niche, normalized for the relative abundance of immune niches. The CD8+ infiltrated and tissue-resident myeloid cell niches in ICI-AIN were most likely to neighbor fibrotic niches compared with the ICI-ATN group ( Figure 4 g). Additionally, we defined a fibrotic niche transcriptional signature as the top 100 differentially expressed genes for the fibrosis niches and calculated a signature score for each immune subniche. Consistent with the neighborhood analysis, the tissue-resident myeloid niches had the highest fibrosis signature score ( Figure 4 h), highlighting their role in a fibrotic tissue response.     Discussion  Here, we have described the landscape of immune infiltration and fibrosis in the kidneys of patients with ICI-AIN versus ICI-ATN. Using high-resolution spatial transcriptomic analysis, we elucidated key features of ICI-AIN, including a strong activation of IFN-γ/STAT1 signaling, a reduction in oxidative phosphorylation in tubular cells, and a heterogeneous immune cell infiltration.  Based on the Tessera algorithm  19   for the identification of niches with similar transcriptional profiles, we were able to identify biologically meaningful, functional units, thereby circumventing the problems associated with cell segmentation. Some niches corresponded to histoanatomical parts of the kidney, like the glomeruli or specific segments of the tubule, allowing us to compare the gene expression within specific kidney regions. Other niche types corresponded to pathological changes, including immune cell infiltration and fibrosis. Clustering-based analyses enabled us to investigate the heterogeneity of the immune cell infiltrate in detail, highlighting how TLS-like structures, myeloid cell-dominant inflammation, and fibrotic processes happen in parallel within the ICI-AIN-damaged kidney. Analyzing the spatial expression of chemokine and/or receptor pairs enabled us to understand the mechanisms that determine the architecture of these meta-structures.  Our analyses found that CD8 +  T cells are associated with the pathogenesis of ICI-AIN given the limited control of ICI-ATN ( Figure 5 ). T cell infiltration appeared to play a functional role in all the immune cell niches we identified, and T cell-related genes were among the most abundant in all niches. These T cells, expressing markers of repeated activation like PD1, CTLA4, and LAG3, seemed to coordinate the recruitment and activation of other immune cells by the expression of CXCL13 (attracting B and T cells and forming TLS-like structures) and IFN-γ (inducing an inflammatory myeloid phenotype). These inflammatory myeloid cells, in turn, may have induced tissue damage by producing metalloproteases like  MMP9  and by recruiting additional CXCR3-expressing inflammatory cells producing CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11.  Figure 5   Schematic of the inferred pathophysiology in ICI-AIN with a focus on the role of CD8 +  T cells. CD8 +  T cells with transcriptional markers of tissue-residency and repeated stimulation are the main producers of IFN-γ. IFN-γ reduces oxidative phosphorylation in kidney tubules and induces a proinflammatory program in myeloid cells. These proinflammatory myeloid cells lead to tissue damage and also produce the chemokines CXCL9, CXCL10, and CXCL11, attracting additional CXCR3 +  lymphocytes, including additional CD8 +  T cells. CD8 +  T cells also produce CXCL13, a chemokine that attracts B cells and induces the formation of tertiary lymphoid structures in the kidney.                       Notably, CD8 +  T cells in ICI-AIN recapitulated features associated with T cells of the tumor microenvironment with transcriptional features of exhaustion and instigation of TLS structures by the production of CXCL13. 30 ,  31 ,  32  Plasma cells also showed increased abundance in the ICI-AIN samples, and we hypothesize that these indicate productive B-T cell interactions in these TLS-like structures. Plasma cells have also been identified in ICI-associated myocarditis; however, no antibodies against myocardial antigens were identified.  12   Although T cells in ICI-ATN samples showed a transcriptional signature typical of short-lived effector cells (expressing  KLRG1  and  CX3CR1 ), the CD8 +  T cells in ICI-AIN expressed more HOBIT ( ZNF683 ), CD103 ( ITGAE ), and CXCR6, markers of tissue-resident memory cells.  33   Interestingly, a CD8 +  T cell subset with high expression of HOBIT was identified in the peripheral blood of a patient with kidney allograft rejection after ICI treatment.  34   A similar signature of  ITGAE  +  tissue-resident T cells was recently reported in ICI-related colitis.  11   It is therefore plausible that CD8 +  tissue-resident memory T cells, disinhibited by ICI treatment, are the primary cell type that initiates the inflammatory cascade observed in ICI-AIN.  Our analyses also implicated niches with a high density of a tissue-resident transcription profile in the development of kidney fibrosis. This is consistent with recent reports highlighting the role of a similar population in fibrotic damage in lupus nephritis.  35   ,   36   Although we reported the spatial association of these niches with fibrotic area, future research is needed to determine if these cells mediate fibrosis or protect against further damage.  The immunological changes we observed may inform the selection of novel treatment targets in ICI-AIN. Currently, ICI-AIN is treated by holding or discontinuing ICIs and administering glucocorticoids, which may compromise anti-tumor immune response.  37   ,   38   Drugs targeting IFN-γ and its receptors, and especially drugs such as baricitinib and ruxolitinib—which target the downstream signaling of Janus Kinase and/or STAT—may thus have greater utility in treating ICI-AIN.  To our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive spatial data of ICI-AKI to date; however, there were limitations. Alignment of kidney structures with spatial transcriptomic areas was poor, and high-resolution images of H&E stainings were performed on serial sections. Furthermore, kidney biopsies from patients with ICI-AIN show great heterogeneity, and the small number of samples analyzed, along with the lack of inclusion of “healthy” controls, may have limited our ability to explore key differences. Notably, medullary cell types and niches were overrepresented in the ICI-AIN samples because of higher representation of kidney medulla in ICI-AIN samples. However, we chose the ICI-ATN group as controls as they share important confounding features with the ICI-AIN group (malignant disease, cancer treatment, and unspecific kidney tissue changes caused by AKI). Additionally, the commercial Xenium 5K panel may have limited utility in providing insight into cell types within the nephron. Methods for cellular segmentation in spatial transcriptomic and proteomic analyses are still an area of active investigation; thus, transcripts of neighboring cells may spill over and dilute marker gene identification, especially in areas with challenging cell morphologies, such as the glomerulus. Current spatial transcriptomic approaches result in relatively sparse data, which can lead to biases. For example, the emphasis on CD8 +  T cells in our data could, at least in part, be explained by the higher transcript density of  CD8A  compared with  CD4 . Although we used a niche-based approach to mitigate these limitations, orthogonal approaches like single-cell transcriptomics in ICI-AIN will be needed to phenotype infiltrating immune cells at higher resolution.  In summary, we used spatial transcriptomics to show that IFN-γ-producing CD8 +  T cells may be implicated in the pathogenesis of ICI-AIN, and that CD8 +  T cell-derived IFN-γ likely induces a proinflammatory state in myeloid cells, with increased tissue production of CXCL9, 10, and 11. Future studies with a larger number of samples will be needed to validate our findings and investigate the association of specific immune niche subsets with disease severity and/or refractoriness, treatment response, and likelihood of kidney recovery. Cross-Modal Training Using Xenium Spatial Transcriptomics Enables DINO-DETR Based Detection of Vascular Niches in H&E Whole-Slide Images <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Tumor vasculature is a key driver of glioma progression, yet routine quantification depends on subjective histopathologic assessment or resource-intensive ancillary immunohistochemistry. A scalable, objective method for vascular phenotyping from routine histology remains an unmet need.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We leveraged 10x Genomics Xenium spatial transcriptomics data from a glioblastoma specimen to generate molecularly resolved annotations of GBM-associated endothelial cells and pericytes across 809,041 cells. These annotations were transferred to matched H&E-stained sections to train a DINO-DETR-based object detection model using a binary classification scheme (vascular vs. other). The model was validated on four independent Xenium patient slides and applied to a retrospective cohort of 119 diffuse gliomas spanning WHO grades 2-4 (oligodendroglioma, astrocytoma, and glioblastoma) with linked survival data.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Binary vascular cell detection achieved a precision of 0.78, a recall of 0.63, and an F1 score of 0.70, with an overall accuracy of 98.6%. Orthogonal spatial validation confirmed that predicted vascular cells were preferentially localized within annotated blood vessel regions. In subtype-stratified survival analysis, high AI-derived vascular cell proportion was significantly associated with worse overall survival in astrocytoma patients (log-rank p < 0.019).</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cross-modal AI training using spatial transcriptomics enables scalable, molecularly informed vascular quantification directly from routine H&E slides. Within the astrocytoma subtype, where tumor grade is most heterogeneous and vascular phenotype most variable, objective vascular quantification provides independent prognostic information demonstrating the potential of spatially supervised deep learning to extract clinically meaningful microenvironmental signals from universally available histologic material.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
